title: Nio launches first fifth-generation battery swap stations - electrive.com
content:
Infrastructure
Nio has opened its first fifth-generation battery swap stations in China. The new stations allow Firefly models to use the swap network for the first time. At the same time, Nio has passed the milestone of 4,000 battery swap stations in its home market.
Nio's battery swap network has now completed more than 120 million battery swaps.
Image: Nio
Nio has opened its first fifth-generation battery swap stations in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Suzhou, Hefei, Chengdu and Quanzhou. The station at Qiaoxiang Gymnasium in Quanzhou is both the first fifth-generation site and Nio’s 4,000th battery swap station in China.
At the heart of the new generation is a swap platform developed in-house by Nio. According to the company, the system adjusts its configuration in real time and locates each vehicle’s battery mounting points precisely. It supports vehicles with wheelbases of up to 3.5 metres, covering models from small cars to large SUVs.
For the first time, vehicles from all three of Nio’s brands – Nio, Onvo and Firefly – can use the same battery swap network. This brings battery swapping to Firefly models for the first time: the roughly four-metre-long electric compact car could not use previous-generation stations because of its shorter wheelbase.
Nio Surpasses 120 Million Battery Swaps
The launch of the new stations coincides with another milestone: Nio completed its 120-millionth battery swap on 7 August. The company had only passed the 100-million mark in early February, meaning it completed another 20 million swaps in around six months.
Nio continues to expand its network. As of 7 August, the company operated 4,006 battery swap stations in China, alongside 5,160 charging stations with a total of 29,801 charging points. Of the swap stations, 1,049 are located along motorways and connect nine north-south and eleven east-west routes as well as 16 major metropolitan areas, according to Nio. The network now covers more than 550 cities.
In urban areas, Nio says 80.1% of its users have at least one battery swap station within three kilometres of their home or workplace.
For now, Nio is focusing the expansion of its battery swap network on its home market in China. The company recently slowed its international expansion and
does not plan to add further battery swap or proprietary charging stations in Europe for the time being
. Instead, it is focusing on partnerships and a less capital-intensive business model. Nio also does not expect to introduce new vehicles based on its 900-volt NT3 platform in Europe before late 2027 or early 2028.
As a result, Nio’s European battery swap network is likely to remain at its current size for the foreseeable future, while the company continues to expand the concept in China. The fifth-generation stations also broaden the network’s reach by allowing models from all three group brands to use the same infrastructure.

title: Neptune Energy advances Altmark lithium project - electrive.com
content:
Neptune Energy is preparing to start lithium production in Germany's Altmark region in 2030. In the second pilot phase, the Hanover-based company and Fraunhofer IEG are now testing different adsorbent materials for future industrial-scale lithium extraction.
Inside the direct lithium extraction pilot plant.
Image: Neptune Energy
After evaluating various direct lithium extraction (DLE) technologies, Neptune Energy is now working with the Fraunhofer Institute for Energy Infrastructures and Geothermal Systems IEG to refine a suitable adsorption process. The ALE (Altmark Lithium Extraction) project aims to extract lithium precursors from deep thermal water in Germany’s Altmark region.
With the project
, Neptune Energy aims to support the domestic supply of critical raw materials. The company plans to gradually start commercial lithium production from 2030 and reach up to 25,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) per year during the 2030s. According to Neptune Energy, that would provide enough lithium for the batteries of around 500,000 electric vehicles annually.
Northern Saxony-Anhalt hosts one of the world’s largest lithium resources associated with a specific project, with proven resources of 43 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent. The lithium is dissolved in thermal water at depths of 3,000 to 4,000 metres and contained in the rock’s fine pore spaces. Neptune Energy plans to bring the thermal water to the surface through wells and extract the lithium using DLE technology.
“During Pilot Phase I last year, we investigated various DLE technologies available worldwide to assess their suitability for the conditions in the Altmark region. Following tests using ion-exchange and adsorption processes, adsorption technology proved to be the most promising for the conditions in the Altmark region. We now intend to further develop this process in collaboration with Fraunhofer IEG,” explained Joachim Sluet, Midstream Manager and head of pilot projects at Neptune Energy.
In the second pilot phase, Neptune Energy and Fraunhofer IEG will test and evaluate different adsorbent materials over the coming months using a DLE pilot plant developed by the institute. The adsorbents selectively bind lithium ions from the thermal water. The lithium is then separated from the material again, resulting in a highly concentrated lithium chloride solution.
“This can be processed in further steps to produce battery-grade lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide monohydrate – the raw material for the European battery and electric mobility industry,” the project initiators state.
For the first test phase, Neptune Energy selected Evonik Catalysts to supply the adsorbent material, which the company says showed high performance and stability in preliminary tests. Evonik is also supporting the pilot programme with on-site process and application expertise.
The pilot plant can process up to 1,000 litres of thermal water per day and extracts the lithium in an oxygen-free environment. It operates three adsorbent columns simultaneously, allowing the adsorption and desorption of lithium ions to take place almost simultaneously, according to the project team.
“The DLE pilot plant developed in collaboration with Fraunhofer IEG is providing us with important insights into selecting the optimal adsorbent material for the brine from the Altmark region. This brings us another step closer to industrial-scale lithium production from the Altmark region,” added Dr Axel Wenke, Director of New Energy & Business Development.
Neptune Energy’s core business is oil and gas production, but the company has been expanding into other areas, including domestic lithium production. According to Neptune Energy, its operations and those of its predecessor companies span more than 135 years. One of those companies, Erdöl Erdgas Gommern, began producing natural gas in the Altmark region in 1969 and was later acquired by Neptune Energy.

title: TU Graz develops guidelines for repairable EV batteries - electrive.com
content:
Researchers at TU Graz have developed design guidelines to make traction batteries safer and easier to repair and recycle. Their analysis shows that repair-friendly designs can pay off economically and environmentally if only 8% of the battery cells are reused.
Symbolic image: The battery of a Porsche Cayenne.
Image: Porsche
A research team led by Graz University of Technology (TU Graz) has compared three battery pack designs to determine how their construction affects safety, repairability and sustainability. The first reflects a common approach using bonded housings and thermally conductive pastes. While such designs have advantages in production, even limited damage can mean replacing the entire battery pack.
The researchers compared this with two designs intended to make repairs easier. One combines replaceable housing covers with heat dissipation pads, while the other uses an electrically insulating oil for liquid cooling and a screwed and sealed housing. The latter allows the battery to be dismantled and individual cells to be replaced.
The work was carried out as part of the E-Track research project and aims to address the lack of standardised designs for traction batteries.
The cells themselves are particularly important when it comes to whether repairs make sense. They account for around 75% of a battery pack’s total mass and are also its biggest cost factor. According to the project’s life-cycle analysis, a repair-friendly design already pays off if 8% of the cells can be reused after an accident. Easier disassembly also makes it simpler to recover materials for recycling.
“Without uniform design standards, emergency services often face major challenges in an emergency because the structure and behaviour of battery systems are difficult to assess. At the same time, we lose valuable resources if batteries cannot be repaired or fully recycled,” said Markus Fasching, project manager at TU Graz’s Vehicle Safety Institute. “Our work shows that safety, efficiency and recyclability can be improved together through well thought-out design.”
E-Track also looked at how damaged cells can be identified before they cause problems. The team developed diagnostic methods combining electrochemical impedance spectroscopy with virtual multiphysics models. The approach can detect internal damage such as micro-shorts, which may otherwise cause a battery fire at a later stage.
Although the project focused primarily on batteries for electric two-wheelers, its methods and simulation approaches are also applicable to larger vehicles, including cars and lorries. The researchers say the results could provide a basis for future industry standards and potentially regulatory frameworks.

title: Schneider Electric launches multi-chemistry battery UPS – Batteries International
content: French multinational Schneider Electric has unveiled a next-generation UPS system that runs on VRLA or lithium ion batteries — and is designed to also support future battery chemistries. Schneider announced the launch of its APC Smart-UPS on August 10 as the industry’s “first monolithic multi-chemistry UPS” for distributed IT and edge environments. The UPS allows the use of VRLA batteries today as a cost-effective option, while customers can move to longer-lasting Li ion when ready — and can then adapt to new battery chemistries as Schneider introduces compatible battery packs. This latest model offers up to 3x the base runtime, up to 1.4x more power density and up to 57% more outlets, while helping reduce power loss by up to 40%, Schneider claims. The platform supports up to 10 external battery packs for extended runtime. Genuine APC batteries maximise the performance and lifespan of the UPS. All have been tested for compatibility and are backed by warranty coverage — in addition to being shipped “factory fresh”, with validated runtime data and support for authorised recycling programmes. The latest APC debuts with the ‘SRTD On-Line’ 2.2kVA and 3kVA series, designed for servers and networking equipment in medical, light industrial, and IT white space applications. Additional capacity models will follow. “Customers shouldn’t have to choose between investing in backup power today and being ready for what comes next,” said Manish Kumar, EVP for secure power and data centres. Last January, Vivek Abrol was appointed MD and CEO of Schneider’s India-based subsidiary, Luminous Power Technologies, succeeding Preeti Bajaj — who moved to lead the global home solutions division of Schneider. title: EU ‘sidelining sustainability in scramble for battery materials’ – Batteries International
content:
Lithium, News, Other Chemistries, Recycling
Read Later
Mining in the DRC. New study says ecological need for reducing demand is 'politically unthinkable'
The European Union is sidelining sustainability principles in the race to secure materials vital to the battery industry, new analysis has claimed.
A study published on August 13, by Germany’s Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ), said security of supply is now taking precedence over sufficiency in raw materials policy.
EU policy continues to focus on securing supplies — ensuring the availability of minerals and metals rather than reducing consumption, the study said.
The study comes after EU environmental policy supremo, Eric Mamer, acknowledged Europe still had work to do in supporting the circular economy — and
the lead battery industry’s near 99% recycling record as a good example of a functioning circular economy business model.
Now UFZ is urging scientists to work more closely with political decision-makers to keep sustainability issues in focus, amid geopolitical tensions and increasing demand for raw materials.
According to UFZ’s study, researchers working at the intersection of ecology, economics, and politics have been warning for some time of the ecological and geopolitical risks posed by rising demand for raw materials.
UFZ’s research team, led by PhD student Theresa Herdlitschka, examined more than 180 publicly available strategy and position papers, press releases and fact sheets published between 2000 and 2024 by key players from politics, industry, academia and NGOs as part of the debate on the future of raw materials.
“By tracing the entire course of the debate, we were able to see which events and interpretations had the greatest influence within the various groups,” Herdlitschka said.
The study found that in the early 2000s, ‘corporate competitiveness’ was initially the dominant narrative in raw materials policy. After the 2007/2008 financial crisis and 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, the narrative of the EU as a ‘pioneer in global environmental protection’ emerged.
In the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine and the energy crisis, this was followed by the narrative of ‘strategic autonomy’.
“Alternative ideas such as sufficiency or reducing demand have continually been sidelined”, Herdlitschka said.
“Even in a context where reducing demand is ecologically necessary, this remains politically unthinkable because the prevailing narrative portrays the problem primarily as a lack of security of supply and competitiveness.”
Herdlitschka said studies on reducing overall raw material consumption or proposals for the prudent use of critical minerals and metals have been proposed by a small group who “failed to get their positions accepted”.
“Demand for raw materials will continue to rise as the geopolitical situation remains tense,” Herdlitschka said.
Scientists now need to work even more closely at the interface between science and policy by engaging directly with political decision-makers — including using the concept of the circular economy and debates on conflicts in the mining sector within the EU to raise the profile of counter-narratives based on local supply chains, sufficiency and social engagement.
UFZ’s study came just weeks after a major new report by Deloitte
buying cheap battery cells from Asia was not a long-term solution for sovereign European battery production.

title: CIP energy projects fund tops $3bn as latest BESS comes online – Batteries International
content: Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners has closed its Growth Markets Fund II at $3 billion, on the heels of starting up its latest BESS facility in the UK. CIP announced the closing of GMF II on August 14. The fund targets large-scale energy infrastructure projects in 15 markets across Eastern Europe, Asia and Latin America. GMF II is nearly triple the size of the first vintage and has already committed around $1.6 billion across nine investments including commissioning of a standalone battery project in Chile and starting construction on Mexico’s first large-scale solar and BESS projects. Niels Holst, partner and co-head of growth markets funds at CIP, said the company had been successful in attracting a diverse group including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds. Meanwhile, on August 12, CIP announced the start of commercial operations of Coalburn 1 in Scotland — a 500MW, two-hour duration BESS, which the company said is currently the largest operational battery in Europe. CIP said the lithium ion BESS will play an important role in strengthening the flexibility and resilience of the UK power system and supporting the continued integration of renewable energy generation. Coalburn 1 is part of CIP’s expanding portfolio of UK energy infrastructure investments. It is one of three transmission-connected BESS assets developed by CIP in Scotland. Together, Coalburn 1, Coalburn 2 and Devilla will provide 1.5GW of power capacity and 3GWh of energy storage. title: CATL strengthens BESS market grip with 3GWh ContourGlobal supply deal – Batteries International
content:
Energy Storage, News
Read Later
ContourGlobal CEO Antonio Cammisecra with LB Tan, CATL's CCO and co-president of sales and marketing
British power generation firm ContourGlobal has signed a 3GWh BESS supply deal for projects in the UK, Greece and Chile with China’s CATL — further consolidating the Asian battery giant’s grip on the international market.
ContourGlobal, which confirmed the deal on August 10, said it marked the first bundle agreement between the two companies and gives it flexibility to align supply as it develops it battery storage portfolio.
Technology at the core of the agreement is a containerised liquid-cooling integrated BESS built around CATL’s large-format LFP cells. The bundle covers a total of 526 containers each rated at 5.64MWh, all configured for four hours of continuous discharge.
The supply agreement covers three recently announced projects: a 500MW / 2,000MWh stand-alone BESS project in Scotland (marking the company’s entry into the UK market), a 100MW / 400MWh facility in Greece and a hybrid project in Chile, which combines 131 MWp PV coupled with 90MW / 360MWh of battery storage.
ContourGlobal said construction of the Chile and Greece projects is already underway, while the Scotland facility is in advanced development.
In addition, the company has a 1.6GW BESS parc under development in Italy, which falls outside the scope of the CATL deal.
Financial details of the agreement were not disclosed, but the partners said CATL’s technology will support BESS installations with its proprietary cell-degradation management system that continuously monitors and mitigates the ageing of each cell.
ContourGlobal said this marks the first use of the tech within its portfolio and brings to its fleet a set of design features including integrated liquid-cooling architecture and built-in fire detection and suppression architecture. This ensures stable operation across a wide range of temperatures and mitigating thermal propagation.
CATL will also take back and recycle units at the end of their useful life, in line with European regulatory requirements.
All of the BESS projects will be equipped to support future grid stability services, including grid-forming functionality where required by system operators.
Although grid-forming services are not yet fully recognised or remunerated under most current regulatory frameworks, the partners said the technology is already designed to enable them as markets evolve.
Antonio Cammisecra, CEO of ContourGlobal, said: “Beyond equipment supply, we are establishing a standardised utility-scale BESS platform across multiple countries, enabling consistent engineering, testing, commissioning and long-term asset management.
“By harmonising technical requirements and project execution practices, we reduce delivery risk, accelerate project deployment and create a scalable model for continued growth of our storage business.”
ContourGlobal, which is backed by international investment firm KKR, is an independent power producer operating across the US, Latin America, Europe and Africa.
The company manages a diversified portfolio of nearly 6GW of renewable generation, flexible thermal power and battery energy storage assets, including 3GWh of operating BESS projects across Europe and the Americas. They include a 202MW / 500MWh stand-alone BESS in Bulgaria, one of the largest in Eastern Europe and in Chile — where the company is operating 2.5GWh of BESS across hybrid projects in the Atacama Desert.
Earlier this year, CATL
the equivalent of $5 billion in a share placement in Hong Kong, pledging to use the cash boost to accelerate construction of new energy projects overseas.
The announcement came just weeks after CATL
reported
near 40% year-on-year growth in global lithium battery sales for 2025.

title: Carlyle-backed Revera kickstarts work on £500m 1GW BESS parc in Scotland – Batteries International
content: Revera Energy has broken ground for its first facility in a planned £500 million ($678 million) 1GW battery storage parc in Scotland. Revera, backed by global investment firm Carlyle, launched site works for its a 200MW / 400MWh Windyhill BESS, northwest of Glasgow, on August 6. The battery chemistry to be used at Windyhill was not specified, but Revera said it represents the first project in the firm’s Scottish BESS portfolio to move into construction. Commercial operations are scheduled for early 2028. The others are Hunterston (400MW / 800MWh) and Kincardine (400MW / 800MWh). Together, the three represent nearly 1GW / 2GWh of capacity. Windyhill reached financial close in February 2026. Windyhill’s technology partner is GE Vernova, with Mitie serving as delivery partner on site. Energy trader Danske Commodities will provide route-to-market services once the facility is operational. Ron Kiecana, acting head of Revera UK and operating partner at Carlyle said: “I’m excited for what lies ahead as we work toward a full gigawatt of storage under construction across Scotland by the year’s end.” Scotland has been at the centre of increasing focus for BESS development, as reported by Batteries International in recent months. In December 2025, the European Marine Energy Centre announced it had successfully completed the first demonstration of tidal power, vanadium flow battery storage and hydrogen as a fully integrated energy system in Scotland’s Orkney islands. Last January, Matrix Renewables said Tesla would design, build and commission a 500MW / 1GWh BESS in Scotland, marking Matrix’s first standalone BESS project in the UK. Matrix is a renewable energy platform created and backed by global alternative asset manager TPG. Most recently, China’s CATL signed a 3GWh BESS supply deal with British power generation firm ContourGlobal for projects including a 500MW / 2,000MWh stand-alone BESS in Scotland — marking the company’s entry into the UK market. title: How Pigment is Reshaping Supply Chain Planning
content:
How Pigment is Reshaping Supply Chain Planning
Prioritise Us
on Google
Éléonore Crespo, CEO and Co-founder of Pigment
Pigment's AI-native platform is reshaping supply chain planning, with a TP deal signalling growing appetite for agent-led enterprise decision-making
Pigment, the AI business planning and performance management platform, is doubling down on supply chain with a suite of
native AI capabilities
designed to surface risk and model disruption in real time, as global digital business services leader TP (formerly Teleperformance) signs on to unify its financial operations across nearly 100 countries on the platform.
The two developments underline a broader shift in how enterprises are approaching planning: moving away from siloed, static spreadsheets and towards connected, AI-driven models that let finance, supply chain and operations teams react at the speed of change.
Forecasting agility for a volatile world
At the centre of Pigment's supply chain capabilities is the ability to build resilience into forecasting by unifying market signals. The platform integrates commercial inputs, macroeconomic indicators and live sales data into a single collaborative forecasting environment, giving teams a high-fidelity view of demand.
Ankorstore, the B2B wholesale marketplace, has already seen measurable gains from the approach. Fabien Gibot, Fulfillment Analyst at Ankorstore, says: "The main KPI we wanted to improve was around forecast accuracy and we improved by 20% to 25%."
Pigment's scenario planning also runs as workflows, allowing supply chain teams to simulate disruptions and stress-test decisions without breaking their baseline.
For manufacturers
navigating volatile trade policy
, that agility has become business-critical. Kate Dolph, Senior Director FP&A and Business Planning at Evenflo, adds: "Tariffs are the single biggest area of focus for Evenflo, we're constantly modelling scenarios to determine how much cost we can absorb. In a fast-changing environment like this, having a tool that lets us rapidly model the P&L impact and pivot our strategy is absolutely essential."
We wanted to improve forecast accuracy and we improved by 20% to 25%.
Fabien Gibot
Fulfillment Analyst at Ankorstore
Pigment's pitch to supply chain leaders is built on three pillars: forecasting agility, aligned decision-making and fast time to value.
The platform is designed to connect teams,
data and scenarios in one place
, so that every function plans, reacts and optimises towards the same outcome, while giving planners the ability to modify and extend their own models as conditions change, rather than waiting on IT.
The platform also aims to remove operational silos by translating supply chain variables directly into corporate KPIs, mapping lead times, shipping volumes and warehouse capacities to cost of goods sold and working capital requirements, so operational decisions are always weighed against margin impact.
AI agents move planning from analysis to action
Underpinning the platform are two purpose-built AI agents. The Analyst Agent analyses supply chain performance, turns operational questions into automated missions and surfaces critical risks at scale, generating reports, scheduling recurring analyses and monitoring key metrics through simple chat interaction.
The Modeler Agent, meanwhile, is built to take planning from idea to production-ready model in minutes, using AI-guided generation to instantly spin up or extend multi-dimensional models, such as adding a new distribution centre or restructuring a supplier network. It can also help teams build optimised board views ahead of cross-functional S&OP meetings.
TP and Pigment will unify and scale the global digital business services leader’s financial operations across nearly 100 countries. Credit: Pigment
TP partnership extends Pigment into global finance operations
The supply chain push comes alongside a significant enterprise win for Pigment in finance. TP, which operates in nearly 100 countries, has selected Pigment to unify its financial planning, statutory consolidation and ESG reporting on a single platform, as part of the group's AI-driven "Future Forward" efficiency programme.
The deal is intended to create a single source of truth across TP's finance function, replacing separate systems for consolidation, planning and reporting with one unified architecture, backed by the controls, audit trails and governance frameworks required of a large publicly listed group.
Pigment said the platform is also designed for continuous evolution, allowing finance teams to modify models, processes and reports themselves as business needs change.
Benoit Gabelle, Interim Group CFO at TP, says: "We were looking for a robust and flexible
platform capable
of helping us enhance finance operations over the long term to accompany our Internal AI / Efficiency program launched within the Future Forward strategic framework.
Benoit Gabelle, Interim Group CFO at TP
"Pigment stood out not only for handling enterprise-scale consolidation, but for their vision of how AI will reshape finance operations. The platform's capacity to evolve and the quality of collaboration throughout the process were key drivers for this decision."
Éléonore Crespo, CEO and Co-founder of Pigment, said: "AI should be embedded directly in the tools and workflows business teams already use, helping them model faster, strengthen performance analysis and identify patterns earlier, so they can make faster and more confident decisions.
"We are very proud to partner with TP, a global leader in digital business services on this journey, as we shape the future of finance together. This partnership is a testament of our ability to handle statutory consolidation for large, multinational corporations together with planning and analysis functions."
The rollout will be supported by specialised partners ReportWise and Silamir, who bring domain expertise to ensure continuity and adoption across the TP Group.
A single thread: AI embedded, not bolted on
Taken together, the TP deal and Pigment's supply chain capabilities point to the same underlying strategy: embedding AI natively into planning workflows across finance, supply chain and operations, rather than treating it as a separate layer.
For enterprises managing volatility across nearly 100 countries or complex, multi-tier supplier networks, that native integration is increasingly being positioned as the difference between reactive and resilient planning.

title: AI and Automation: Exploring GXO's Robotics Adoption
content:
AI and Automation: Exploring GXO's Robotics Adoption
Prioritise Us
on Google
GXO uses a range of adaptive technologies, AI and robotics to streamline logistics. Credit: GXO
GXO Logistics is incorporating AI across its end-to-end solutions, making use of automation and robotics to help its customers develop greater efficiency
GXO Logistics
is helping companies around the world with their business growth, resilience and operational agility.
It is undertaking a technological transformation, through robotics and AI in order to better support its clients and partners.
The organisation is seeing increases in efficiency, worker safety and productivity across the supply chain.
A modern logistics issue
The logistics industry is a complex one, reliant on thousands of moving parts at any given time. A single disruption can cause huge amounts of monetary loss, delay operations and cause shutdowns.
Within the industry, visibility and coordination is critical – meaning hand offs operate seamlessly, finance teams are in constant communication with manufacturing leads, partners and carriers are kept in the loop at all time. Failed hand offs or poor visibility can destroy customer trust or result in major workflow disruption.
In recent years – due to the rise of ecommerce, increasing supplier diversification and growing volatility – the logistics industry has been undertaking a significant transformation. What was once reliant on manual data uploads, spreadsheets, faxes and phone calls, is now a system which cannot operate as it once did.
Now, the workflow relies on automation, AI and orchestration platforms. The industry is becoming more automated, working to fill the gap of supply and demand, meet time-sensitive tasks, reduce long-term costs and meet the increasing skills gap.
GXO Logistics, multinational contract logistics company which span off from XPO Logistics in 2021, has been increasingly adopting
AI and automation
across its solutions, in order to meet consumer demand and help its partners operate with efficiency and resilience.
"GXO Logistics, Inc. is incorporating AI throughout our supply chain end-to-end solutions," says Jacob Huynh, Business Development expert at GXO, on LinkedIn.
Jacob Huynh, Business Development at GXO Logistics
"Tools like GXO IQ and automated robotics are already shaping how we help CPG and retail brands run smarter, more resilient supply chains."
AI implementation
Understanding that every supply chain faces unique issues, with different operations and capabilities, GXO uses tailored solutions to help navigate complexity. It operates across a broad range of logistics expertise, including manufacturing, warehousing, distribution and
reverse logistics
The company makes use of robotics and AI tools to help it better meet demand and pace of the supply chain industry. In 2025, the company introduced GXO IQ – a logistics platform to help the company execute, optimise and scale. It uses machine learning models which offer accurate predictions and real-time data solutions to inform confident decision making.
It is a context-aware AI model which adapts to the conditions and needs of each site, built for rapid deployment and efficient onboarding. It has a single view layer for everyone, whether they are an operator, executive or customer. It helps across operations execution, AI operations orchestration and uses a thorough network to provide a rich data layer.
As a company, GXO welcomes AI, using it across its operations, but also using its operations to help the growth of AI. It has operations in 26 countries, helping across a range of industries, including data centres.
In recent years, the AI demand has driven a huge growth in data centres, and GXO has been helping that with specific warehouses to store parts and has solutions to transport them to the necessary place.
"We're on all parts of the AI equation," explained
Patrick Kelleher
, CEO of GXO, to CNBC.
Patrick Kelleher, CEO, GXO Logistics
"We're on the data centre build, helping build the capacity to run AI, and we are a big adopter of AI. We launched a tool, GXO IQ, last year, which is the medium for us to deploy the AI to our 1,200 operations across the world.
"We're seeing great results from AI – we implemented an AI bot to improve picking productivity for our consumer manufacturing and saw a 50% improvement in productivity.
"We use AI for forecasting to understand what the demand is going to be, day to day and hour to hour, so we can plan our labour in the right way. We use it to help our customers deploy inventory and to make sure it gets processed throughout the warehouse in an efficient way."
A helping hand
GXO has a selection of
advanced automation
, automated sorting capabilities, intelligent robots and more, all operating to ensure efficiency and accuracy across the supply chain. In its warehouses, cobots and employees work side by side, resulting in significant productivity improvement. Robotic arms are implemented across lines, performing repetitive movements with significant precision. From building pallets to engraving products, these arms can be tailored to suit any task and workload.
"I'm super passionate about humanoid robotics playing a big role in the warehouses going forward," added Patrick. "We've done 45 pilots with six different providers. We already have humanoids doing tasks in the warehouse, such as picking cosmetics or unloading trucks."
GXO uses a range of large scale automation in its centres (Credit: GXO)
Tools like GXO IQ and automated robotics are already shaping how we help CPG and retail brands run smarter, more resilient supply chains.
Jacob Huynh, Business Development expert at GXO
In April, the company implemented the first autoload system in Europe. This increases workplace safety, throughput and enhances operational standards.
Around the world, GXO has been developing digital warehouses, designed as collaborative environments which work to help companies operate more efficiently and
more sustainably
In France, the logistics expert has been trialling vision technology, improving speed and accuracy during picking, with real-time communication capabilities. In the US, it has piloted the ProGlove intelligent scanner, which offers real-time information about products and inventory levels, helping reduce time, increase efficiency and supporting worker wellbeing.
GXO is welcoming the age of technology with its advancements in AI and automation, working to transform the logistics sector into a more efficient and technologically adept industry.

title: Tesla 'flying' Roadster demo could come this month, with no one inside
content:
New Tesla Roadster
Fred Lambert
| Aug 14 2026 - 8:43 am PT
Tesla is planning to finally show its new Roadster as early as this month, and the event is supposed to include a stunt where the car lifts off the ground, according to a new report from
The Information
(paywall).
There’s a catch. The car will be operated remotely with nobody in it, and spectators will be kept several hundred yards back because the SpaceX-developed cold gas thrusters are loud enough to damage their eardrums.
The demo keeps shrinking
The demonstration is planned for SpaceX’s rocket test site in McGregor, Texas, three people familiar with the plans told The Information. We reported based on another The Information report in June that Tesla had
pushed the Roadster demo to August
while the thruster package, internally code-named A71, was still being worked out.
A few months ago, the plan was a lot wilder. Tesla wanted the Roadster to race up a magnetized roller-coaster-style ramp, drive upside down, right itself, and hover, according to the report. Tesla previewed that version to Elon Musk, delayed it, and has since cut some of it back.
Musk has been managing expectations internally. He told staff in recent weeks that the demo will be hard to pull off and could go wrong, but that it will be entertaining either way, one person said.
Whether Tesla streams it live or releases edited footage afterward couldn’t be learned.
The car Musk actually picked
The report also fills in years of gaps in how the Roadster got here.
In 2022, two groups inside Tesla’s design studio were working on completely different cars. One was figuring out what a Roadster built on the Model S Plaid’s structure and components would look like, basically a stretched version of the 2017 prototype. The team tore a Model S apart to study the possibility. The other group started from scratch around an ultralight carbon fiber tub, the way top-end performance cars and race cars are built.
Musk picked the carbon tub and told staff to “do it correctly or not at all,” according to one person familiar with his comments. That killed the option of reusing Tesla’s existing vehicle architecture, which has since been discontinued anyway, and committed the company to building a real hypercar, which required engineering expertise Tesla didn’t have. It hired engineers out of Italy, including Stefan Nothdurfter, a former head of body engineering at Lamborghini. He has since moved on from Tesla.
The styling went through a Lamborghini Countach phase, a favorite of design chief Franz von Holzhausen. He later told the team he wanted the car to evoke the Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird spy plane, which is where the A-71 code name comes from. By 2025 the design had settled into something more conservative that pulled from the Countach work, and Tesla built a running two-seat prototype with butterfly doors late last year. Von Holzhausen
said last week that the Roadster is coming “very soon.”
The flying part shrank along the way too. “We started off thinking we were almost making an aircraft and ended up with something closer to hovering,” one person with knowledge of the program said.
The limited edition isn’t really a car
The limited edition Tesla plans to demo in Texas won’t be street legal and will likely cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, if not millions, according to the report. Tesla has internally discussed selling it to a handful of superfans through a program modeled on Ferrari’s XX Programme, where owners drive track-only cars under supervision.
Tesla also toyed with making it a single-seater, putting a cold gas thruster where the passenger seat goes. As currently designed, a person most likely can’t drive it while the thrusters are firing. Too loud.
And the people who actually paid are still waiting. Tesla took $50,000 reservations for the standard Roadster and $250,000 for the Founders Series in 2017, and it has moved the goalpost at least eight times since. Marques Brownlee and Sam Altman have both said publicly they canceled. Musk jokes about the “long-suffering” reservation holders at shareholder meetings.
The company
filed new Roadster trademarks in May
, which is the closest thing to hard evidence of progress anyone outside Tesla has seen in a while.
Electrek’s Take
If this report is true, who the hell asked for this? Tesla owes 100s of Roadsters to early adopters and people who paid in full a decade ago.
The version Tesla is about to show off can’t be sold to the public, can’t be driven with its main party trick running, and will cost more than most houses. That’s not a product. It’s a commercial for Musk’s ability to do things nobody asked for, staged at a rocket facility, with an empty driver’s seat because the car might blow out your eardrums.
I guess that’s Tesla in a nutshell today. More demo than product. Just like the Robotaxi.

title: Ferrari CZ26: what if the Luce had a baby with a SF90
content:
Ferrari Luce
Ferrari SF90 Stradale PHEV
Fred Lambert
| Aug 14 2026 - 7:13 am PT
Ferrari rolled out a new one-off at Monterey called the CZ26, and the face of it looks a lot like the brand’s first electric car. Underneath, it’s an SF90 Stradale plug-in hybrid with a 7.9 kWh battery and 25 km of electric range.
So Ferrari built something that wears the Luce’s design language on top of a twin-turbo V8. Basically, what you’d get if the Luce and the SF90 had a baby.
What Ferrari actually built
The CZ26 came out of Ferrari’s Special Projects program, the commission service that turns a single client’s brief into a car. This one was designed by the Ferrari Design Studio under Flavio Manzoni for a US buyer, and Ferrari says these projects take about two years from idea to finished car.
Mechanically, nothing changed. Ferrari kept the SF90 Stradale’s full spec sheet: a 3,990 cc twin-turbo V8 rated at 797 cv, electric motors good for 162 kW, a 7.9 kWh battery, 328 km/h top speed, and 0-100 km/h in 2.5 seconds.
The emissions line in Ferrari’s own spec table: 154 g/km on the WLTP cycle, with a 68-liter fuel tank and 25 km of electric-only range.
Everything above the hard points is new. The CZ26 gets a two-box silhouette, a central “capsule” volume with the wheel arches pushed out as separate muscular elements, a truncated tail with cantilevered taillights, redesigned front cooling with bypass ducts, air curtains in the bumper corners, a new rear spoiler and diffuser, and a silver Argento Veloce paint with a liquid effect.
The Luce’s face on a combustion car
Look at the front. Ferrari describes it as a full-width functional grille with ultra-slim lighting modules designed for a “concealed effect,” with sensors and brake ducts integrated into the same band.
That’s the visual grammar of the
Ferrari Luce, the brand’s first EV
: horizontal emphasis, lighting hidden inside a full-width graphic, clean surfaces with the functional bits emerging out of them instead of being bolted on. Ferrari even uses the same black-roof-and-pillars trick to make the cabin read as a capsule dropped into the body.
And Ferrari’s release says the CZ26 draws on “the most significant examples of Italian industrial design from the 1970s.”
The Luce got hammered when it was revealed in Rome in May, with former Ferrari chairman Luca di Montezemolo telling Italian media to “at least take the prancing horse off” and the stock dropping as much as 8% in the days after. Ferrari didn’t blink. It
sold the entire ~500-unit 2026 allocation
at €550,000 (~$640,000) in under two months, and CEO Benedetto Vigna said
orders kept coming despite the backlash
Now some of the same design cues are popping up are on a mid-engine supercar. That’s not a retreat.

New Jersey
Micah Toll
| Aug 14 2026 - 6:42 am PT
When New Jersey passed one of the country’s most restrictive e-bike laws earlier this year, plenty of riders, advocates, and bike shops warned that it would have consequences. Now, just a few weeks after the law officially took effect, those predictions appear to have come true.
Bike shops across the state are
reporting
declines in e-bike sales ranging from 20% to an astonishing 90%, with many saying customers are simply deciding that owning an e-bike in New Jersey is no longer worth the hassle.
The law, which
took effect on July 19
, requires every e-bike in the state to be registered, from the slowest Class 1 pedal-assist models all the way through faster Class 3 bikes. Riders under 17 without a driver’s license must pass an MVC licensing test to obtain a special e-bike license, while Class 2 throttle-equipped e-bikes and Class 3 models also require insurance, similar to owning a car.
The result has been widespread confusion. Some customers reportedly believe e-bikes have simply been banned outright. Others tell dealers they’ll just buy online and ignore the requirements. And many are choosing not to buy an e-bike at all.
The impact on local businesses has been severe. One New Jersey dealer said sales plunged 90%, another reported a 63% decline, while others described losing between 20% and 60% of their e-bike business. Several shops have already laid off employees, closed rental operations, downsized, or warned they may not survive through the end of the year.
Perhaps most troubling are the unintended consequences for the very people e-bikes help the most. Dealers who specialize in mobility-focused transportation say disabled customers are returning newly purchased e-bikes or abandoning plans to buy them altogether because they fear they won’t qualify for licensing or insurance requirements. One retailer described customers losing transportation to work or school because of the new rules.
What’s particularly frustrating is that many of these problems
were predictable
. The law treats a low-speed 15-20 mph (25-32 km/h) throttle-equipped Class 2 e-bike much more like a motorcycle than like a bicycle, despite its similar performance to a standard Class 1 pedal-assist bike. Bike shops and advocacy groups have instead urged lawmakers to exempt low-speed e-bikes under 20 mph (32 km/h) from licensing, registration, and insurance requirements while focusing regulation on higher-speed, higher-powered machines that more closely resemble electric mopeds.
It’s hard to argue with that logic. If the goal was to improve safety, discouraging people from riding bicycles and pushing them back into cars seems like an odd way to do so, especially when cars are the very things supposedly making e-bikes “unsafe”.
Electrek’s Take
I’ve been
warning about this
ever since the bill was proposed. Laws like these might sound reasonable if you’re only thinking about the handful of reckless riders making headlines, but in practice, they end up sweeping ordinary e-bike riders into a regulatory mess that makes cycling less attractive.
The numbers coming out of New Jersey are exactly what many of us feared: fewer e-bike sales, fewer people riding, struggling local bike shops, and mobility options disappearing for people who depend on them.
There’s absolutely a conversation to be had about regulating high-speed electric motorcycles masquerading as bicycles. But requiring registration, licensing, and insurance for low-speed e-bikes that have been safely sharing bike paths for years is a solution that appears to have created far more problems than it solved.

content:
Markets & Policy
In other news, the Schleswig-Holstein Ministry of Energy Transition reportedly confirmed the cancellation of the 2.1 GW HyScale 100 electrolyzer project at a German refinery, with a lack of planning certainty cited among the reasons.
Power to Hydrogen has begun installing a 500 kW AEM electrolyzer in Antwerp, while Hystar and BHEL are partnering on local PEM electrolyzer manufacturing in India, and Italy has launched a €400 million annual renewable hydrogen support scheme.
Sergio Matalucci
14 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Highlights
Hydrogen
Image: NEOM
Neom Green Hydrogen Company
started the commissioning of the 2.2 GW green hydrogen and ammonia project in Saudi Arabia. “The plant remains on track with our 4 GW solar and wind power generation sites to be completed by mid-2026, followed by commissioning of the electrolysers, with expected product availability in 2027,” stated the company. In March, NGHC that construction was 90% complete across all sites. The joint venture is the result of a collaboration between Acwa, Air Products and Neom. The wind/PV-powered plant in Saudi Arabia will produce up to 600 tonnes per day of green hydrogen. China’s Sungrow
recently said
that it will provide its inverter skid technology and 1+X modular inverter solution for the project.
Schleswig-Holstein Ministry of Energy Transition
reportedly confirmed that the partners in HyScale 100 have canceled the 2.1 GW electrolyzer project planned at the Heide refinery in the German state. According to local media outlet
, the refinery cited a lack of planning certainty, among other factors, as the reason for canceling the wind-powered hydrogen production plant. Holcim, another project partner alongside Ørsted and Hynamics, reportedly said that the cancellation would not affect its other projects. The federal and state governments had allocated nearly €900 million to the project,
reported. “In September 2025, we received information from the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs that the last remaining project partner, Hynamics, would not be continuing with the project. Schleswig-Holstein had promised funding as initial support,” confirmed the Schleswig-Holstein Ministry to
pv magazine
, adding that state funds amounting to approximately 194 million euros had been reserved by Schleswig-Holstein. “However, these funds were never disbursed and have since been released. Accordingly, no financial damage has been incurred by Schleswig-Holstein”.

(P2H2) has delivered and begun installing a 500 kW anion exchange membrane (AEM) electrolyzer at the
Port of Antwerp-Bruges
in Belgium. “The project is the world’s first to utilize 250 kW AEM electrolyzer stacks and, once commissioned, will be the first AEM system to demonstrate renewable hydrogen production in a high-throughput industrial port environment under real operating conditions,”
the AEM electrolyzer systems developer. The system offers a sub-50-millisecond response for renewable load-following and pressurized operation. “By pairing performance with a lower-cost materials pathway, the company’s AEM systems can reduce Capex costs by up to 65% versus comparable PEM electrolyzers.” The public launch is planned for September.

and India’s

Fredrik Mowill, CEO of Hystar.

title: When heat becomes a stress test: What extreme temperatures mean for photovoltaic systems and battery storage - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Photovoltaics rely on sunlight. Battery storage systems rely on absorbing and releasing energy precisely when the power grid needs it. Both sound like an ideal combination for hot summer days: plenty of sunshine, high generation, increased electricity demand due to cooling, and greater grid flexibility. In practice, it’s more complex.
Andreas Kern and Philippe Staudinger from Meteocontrol
14 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Image: Meteocontrol
Heat waves in Europe are becoming the norm. Strong sunlight isn’t the problem. The critical factor is temperature. Solar modules are evaluated under standard test conditions: 1,000 watts per square meter of irradiance and a cell temperature of 25 degrees Celsius. In the field, cell temperatures on hot days are significantly higher. Modules can get considerably hotter than the ambient air temperature.
In crystalline solar cells, power output typically decreases with increasing temperature. If the cell temperature is not 25 degrees Celsius but 65 degrees Celsius, this corresponds to a power loss of approximately 16 percent compared to standard conditions, assuming a temperature coefficient of minus 0.4 percent per degree.
For operators, this distinction is crucial. Those who only look at raw yield figures are missing the bigger picture. The more important question is: did the photovoltaic system produce as it should under the actual irradiance and temperature conditions?
Extreme temperatures are rarely the sole cause of a problem. Often, they reveal existing weaknesses. These include, among other things, dirty modules, partial shading, vegetation, and damaged cell areas. Under high irradiance, current flows and thermal stresses increase. Small imbalances can therefore become more apparent.
A typical example is hotspots. These occur when individual cell areas are subjected to higher loads than the rest of the module. Under strong irradiance, a local electrical effect can turn into a thermal problem.
Battery storage makes the system question more complex
With battery storage, the issue of heat becomes even more relevant, as it changes the operating logic of the entire system. A storage system can absorb excess solar energy, smooth feed-in peaks, reduce curtailment, shift electricity to more valuable hours, provide grid services, and stabilize load profiles. This is precisely why storage is becoming increasingly important in markets with a high share of photovoltaics.
But energy storage devices have their own physics: lithium-ion batteries age through calendar aging and cycle aging. Temperature, state of charge, depth of discharge, C-rate, idle times, and operating strategy all influence how quickly capacity and performance decline. Studies clearly show that high temperatures, high states of charge, and deep cycles can accelerate aging.
Heat also affects storage systems on several levels. Cooling systems have to work harder, self-consumption increases, and thermal reserves decrease. Battery systems can reduce their performance when cell, rack, or container temperatures reach critical limits. At the same time, prolonged periods of high temperature and high state of charge can accelerate calendar aging.
This is particularly relevant in photovoltaic-coupled applications, where storage systems are quickly charged at midday and then remain at a high state of charge and high ambient temperature for hours.
Safety is also a key issue. Modern battery systems feature battery management systems, temperature sensors, fire protection concepts, and shutdown logic. Nevertheless, thermal runaway remains a significant risk. Studies indicate that an internal cell defect after leaving the manufacturing process cannot be completely ruled out by operational technology. Therefore, it is crucial to prevent propagation, measure off-gas, and design and operate systems in such a way that a single fault does not become a systemic event.
Photovoltaics and storage must be considered together.
In hybrid systems, two effects converge: the photovoltaic system produces substantial energy under high irradiance but loses some of its potential output due to high cell temperatures. The storage system is intended to absorb surplus energy, shift peak loads, and stabilize the power grid, but it too is subjected to greater stress due to high temperatures.
This creates conflicting objectives in operation. A storage system can be fully charged at midday, even though the ambient temperature is high. It can remain at a high charge level for hours. It can be heavily discharged in the evening while cooling, grid load, and price signals are all at play. Each of these decisions can be economically sound. Or it can become expensive in the long run.
Therefore, what matters is not a single operating mode, but the continuous evaluation of use cases. The potential gains from trading, optimizing self-consumption, or grid services must be constantly weighed against efficiency losses, thermal stress, and additional aging. Modern energy management systems perform this task and continuously reassess technical conditions, market and grid signals, and derive the appropriate operating strategy from this analysis. Here’s what operators should pay attention to:
1. Heat logic begins with plant design
Shading is generally detrimental to solar panels because it reduces yield, exacerbates mismatch effects, and can promote hotspots. However, targeted shading can be beneficial for battery storage systems because it reduces thermal stress and eases the load on the cooling system.
This sounds trivial, but in practice it quickly becomes a real conflict of objectives. What yields maximum output for the photovoltaic area is not automatically the best solution for storage containers, inverters, transformer stations or switch cabinets.
Therefore, the design of a system should also consider how the system behaves on hot days. Where do heat build-up occur? Which components are permanently exposed to direct sunlight? How well are storage systems, inverters, and electrical infrastructure ventilated or shaded? How easily accessible are critical components for maintenance, inspection, and fire department access?
Test regulatory capacity under stress conditions
For photovoltaic-plus-storage systems, it’s not enough to simply check whether individual components are functioning. The crucial factor is whether the system as a whole remains controllable when multiple demands are at play simultaneously: high irradiance, high temperatures, grid requirements, storage strategy, inverter limits, and economic operating schedules.
Operators should therefore not only evaluate the control concept on paper, but also validate it in operation. Are setpoints reliably adopted? Does the system react correctly to specifications at the grid connection point? Do active and reactive power control function even under high load? Are ramp rates maintained? Is storage operation adjusted if temperature, state of charge, or derating limits contraindicate it? And is it clearly documented when and why the system was regulated or curtailed?
3. Data quality is the basis of every evaluation.
The next step is a clean data foundation. Irradiance, ambient temperature, module temperature, wind, inverter data, string data, battery temperatures, state of charge and operating conditions must be plausible.
Faulty sensors lead to incorrect diagnoses. Incorrect diagnoses lead either to unnecessary call-outs or to overlooked problems.
4. Performance must be evaluated with temperature correction.
Operators should also use comparison logic. Individual strings, inverters, tracker sections, subsystems, or storage containers should be compared against similar units over the same period.
If all areas react similarly to heat, this suggests a general temperature effect. If individual areas differ significantly, this indicates a local problem.
5. Consistently prioritize local risks
Hotspots, shading, and pollution should be consistently prioritized. Especially under high solar irradiance, local effects can have a greater impact. Vegetation control, cleaning strategies, thermography, and visual inspection should therefore not be considered in isolation, but rather as part of a comprehensive risk management strategy. Electrical infrastructure also deserves more attention: connectors, cables, junction boxes, distribution boxes, switch cabinets, and transformers are all subject to stress during periods of heat.
6. Storage devices need thermal transparency
For battery storage systems, good operation begins with thermal transparency. Cell, module, rack, and container temperatures must not only be measured but also evaluated in context. Not only is the absolute maximum temperature is relevant, but also the temperature distribution. Large temperature variations within a system can indicate cooling problems, airflow issues, sensor malfunctions, or uneven load distribution.
7. Consciously control charge level and aging
State-of-charge (SOC) windows should be carefully selected. A storage system doesn’t need to be constantly maintained near 100 percent SOC just because a lot of photovoltaic energy is available. Especially at high ambient temperatures, it can be beneficial to design operating strategies so that high SOCs aren’t maintained unnecessarily long.
The cooling system must also be treated like a critical component. HVAC or liquid cooling systems are not secondary components. They ensure performance, lifespan, and safety. Filters, air ducts, refrigerants, compressors, pumps, sensors, and redundancies must be included in maintenance plans.
8. Take early indicators and alarms seriously
Important early indicators also include: increasing temperature differences between racks, noticeable cell voltage deviations, increasing internal resistance, decreasing round-trip efficiency, more frequent derating, unexpected SOC drifts, communication errors, or unusual HVAC runtimes.
A single signal does not constitute an emergency. Together, they can form a pattern.
9. Systematically follow up on heat waves
After a heat wave, the system should not automatically return to normal operation. Hot days provide valuable data: Which inverters derated first? Which strings showed deviations? Which sensor data was implausible? Which storage areas exhibited unusual thermal activity? Which alarms were helpful, and which were just noise? Such analyses lead to improved operation.
What we as an industry can learn from this
Heat waves are therefore more than just a seasonal extreme. They are a practical test of whether photovoltaic, storage, and hybrid systems can be understood and managed throughout their entire life cycle. Systematic evaluation of such phases provides insights not only into individual components but also into the quality of the overall operating model.
About the authors
Andreas Kern is a Senior Technical Consultant. His responsibilities include providing technical consulting services within the Technical Consulting department. These services include, for example, yield assessments, technical inspections, technical due diligence, and BESS yield assessments
Philippe Staudinger is Technical Director at mc Energy and is responsible for building and developing the technical organization. He also shapes the operational structures in the C&I energy sector and focuses on the development and implementation of decentralized battery energy storage systems (BESS) for commercial and industrial customers

title: KIT develops hybrid solar system with radiative cooling - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
KIT researchers have developed a hybrid system that combines photovoltaics and passive radiative cooling to simultaneously generate electricity, heat, and cooling from a single surface. A prototype achieved cooling of up to 6.5 C below ambient temperature, 60.6 W/m² of electrical power density, and heat temperatures of up to 110.8 C.
Sandra Enkhardt
14 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Prototype of a hybrid radiative cooling and solar system for simultaneous electricity generation, heating, and cooling. | Image: Gan Huang / KIT
Photovoltaic systems for electricity, solar thermal collectors for heat, and air conditioning for cooling are standard solutions for buildings. Researchers at the
Karlsruhe Institute of Technology
(KIT) have developed a hybrid system designed to provide all three simultaneously from a single surface. The system combines solar energy harvesting with the cold of outer space through passive daytime
radiative cooling
Radiative cooling
occurs when the surface of an object absorbs less radiation from the atmosphere and emits more. As a result, the surface loses heat and a cooling effect can be achieved without the need for power.
The hybrid system integrates photovoltaics with PDRC. Its core component is a light-transmitting cooling layer that radiates heat into space as infrared radiation. The transparent layer consists of a silicon dioxide plate coated with the silicone polymer polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). It allows sunlight to pass through for photovoltaic generation while simultaneously emitting heat into space through the “atmospheric window,” a wavelength range in which the Earth’s atmosphere is particularly transparent to thermal radiation.
Behind the cooling layer, a Fresnel lens concentrates sunlight onto a small photovoltaic-thermal collector, which generates both electricity and heat.
The research team tested the system prototype in outdoor conditions. The device achieved cooling of up to 6.5 C below ambient temperature, an electrical power density of 60.6 W/m², and temperatures of up to 110.8 C for heat utilization.
The main challenge was integrating two competing processes: the solar collector must absorb as much solar energy as possible, while the radiative cooling component needs to remain as cool as possible.
“We solved this problem by having sunlight first pass through the transparent cooling layer, with a Fresnel lens positioned beneath it to focus the light onto a much smaller solar collector,” said Iván Alberto Cruz García, a doctoral researcher and lead author of the study at KIT’s Institute of Microstructure Technology. “This keeps the hot solar collector and the cooling layer physically separated.”
The development builds on research conducted at KIT in 2024, when researchers developed a transparent material capable of passively cooling buildings while allowing daylight to pass through. “Building on that, we have now supplemented the radiative cooling function with a component for solar energy harvesting. This transforms a single surface into a multifunctional energy system,” said co-author Gan Huang.
The researchers presented their findings in the study “Co-harvesting universe coldness and solar energy for tri-generation of cooling, electricity and heating,” published in
Cell Reports Physical Science
The team plans to optimize sunlight guidance, thermal management, and the solar cells. “Our vision is for roofs and facades to become active energy surfaces that simultaneously provide electricity, heat, and cooling,” said Huang. The concept could also be relevant to energy-intensive applications such as AI data centers, which require substantial amounts of electricity and cooling.
Radiative cooling was recently applied to solar panel cooling by researchers from
Shanghai Jiao Tong University
in China,
Purdue University
in the United States, the
Catalan Institute of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology and the Instituto de Ciencia de Materiales
in Spain, and the
Jordan University of Science and Technology and the Australian College of Kuwait

title: Chinese PV Industry Brief: Longi plans 100 MW perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell pilot line - pv magazine Global
content: Longi plans to invest CNY 203.53 million ($29.9 million) to build a 100 MW pilot production line for high-efficiency crystalline silicon-perovskite tandem solar cells. The project will occupy 4,000 m2 at an existing pilot facility within Longi’s Central R&D Institute. The company will lease space and use supporting equipment from the existing facility, while installing new equipment for perovskite thin-film deposition, rapid perovskite crystallization and functional-layer thin-film deposition. The pilot line will support research and development and pilot production of high-efficiency crystalline silicon-perovskite tandem cells. The Chinese PV manufacturer has steadily advanced its crystalline silicon-perovskite tandem technology in recent years. In 2023, it reported a certified efficiency of 33.5%, followed by a 33.9% world record later that year and 34.6% in 2024. The company raised the record to 34.85% in April 2025 and, most recently, to 35.5% in July 2026 , setting a new world record for the technology. The result was independently certified by the European Solar Test Installation (ESTI). Tongwei issued an update on Aug. 11 regarding its planned acquisition of Lihao Clean Energy. The company plans to acquire a 100% stake in polysilicon manufacturer Lihao Clean Energy from 57 shareholders, including Duan Yong, Hainan Zhuoyue and Hainan Haoyue, through a combination of share issuance and cash payment. Tongwei also plans to raise supporting funds through a share placement to no more than 35 qualified investors. According to the announcement, the audit, valuation and other preliminary work related to the transaction has largely been completed, and the acquisition has entered the final stage of negotiations over the transaction plan. Qinghai Lihao is a privately held joint-stock company registered in 2021 in Xining, Qinghai province. Its business scope includes electronic materials and related manufacturing and trading activities. Industry reports describe Lihao as a rapidly scaling polysilicon producer leveraging Qinghai’s renewable power resources. Public reporting on its buildout indicates that a first-phase 50,000 metric ton polysilicon project reached commissioning in 2022, with longer-term capacity ambitions reported to be significantly higher, although Tongwei’s suspension notice did not disclose capacity figures or a purchase price. Trina Solar released an investor relations activity record dated Aug. 7, 2026, on Aug. 11. The company said it has adopted a dual-driver TOPCon 3.0 + THBC strategy for its module business. Its THBC products will target high-value rooftop markets and are expected to enter mass production in the second half of 2026. Trina also said it expects perovskite tandem cells to enter small-scale production in 2028-29, with GW-scale capacity targeted for 2029. PV industry research firm InfoLink released its global cell shipment ranking for the first half of 2026 on Aug. 10. The top five cell manufacturers shipped a combined 91.9 GW, up 5% year on year. Tongwei ranked first, followed by Yingfa Ruineng, SolarSpace, Jietai Technology and Sunsync. title: What makes women join, stay and progress in Solar+? - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
This week, Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) announces its first contribution to SolarPower Europe’s Solar Jobs Report 2026. The article will explore women’s representation across the Solar+ industries and the factors influencing their attraction, retention and career progression. But to tell that story, WiSEu needs data, and this is where your voice is needed.
Women in Solar+ Europe
14 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Image: WiSEU
The energy transition is creating millions of jobs worldwide. Yet measuring progress only through the number of positions created provides an incomplete picture. As the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) highlights in its
Renewable Energy and Jobs: Annual Review 2025
, attention must also be paid to job quality, security, career prospects and whether opportunities are distributed fairly.
We often assume that career opportunities and progression are determined primarily by skills, experience and performance. In practice, however, the environments in which those decisions are made also play an important role.
IRENA’s latest gender research shows that women hold 32% of full-time renewable energy jobs. However, they remain concentrated in administrative positions, while their participation declines to 28% in STEM-related roles and only 19% in senior management and board positions. IRENA identifies cultural and organisational norms, rather than a lack of skills or interest, as significant barriers to women’s participation and advancement.
These figures tell us something important about where we are, but they do not tell us enough about what happens throughout women’s careers or the workplace conditions behind those numbers.
What attracts women to Solar+ in the first place? What makes them stay? What helps them progress? How important are flexibility, communication, workplace culture, leadership and access to career opportunities? And can women see themselves building a long-term career in our industries?
These are some of the questions we want to explore in our article for the European Solar Jobs Report 2026. Rather than relying solely on existing research, we want to build part of the article from the experiences of women working across Solar+ today.
Five minutes to help us build the data
Women in Solar+ Europe is launching a
short survey for women
working across solar, energy storage, EV charging, grid infrastructure and the wider ecosystem supporting these industries.
The survey explores what attracted women to the sector and the factors influencing their decisions to stay and progress, including career opportunities, workplace flexibility, communication, inclusion, leadership and professional development. It takes approximately five minutes to complete.
Responses will be analysed collectively and transformed into original insights for our article in SolarPower Europe’s Solar Jobs Report 2026. This will allow us to complement existing representation figures with a deeper understanding of the experiences behind the numbers.
For WiSEu, this is also only the beginning. One of the challenges we continue to encounter when discussing women’s representation is the lack of data available to understand where action is most needed. We want to help close that gap by progressively building an evidence base that supports better-informed decisions across our industries.
The energy transition is ultimately about more than capacity, investment and cost. It is also about people, human well-being and the quality of the jobs being created. Building an inclusive workforce therefore requires us to understand not only who enters the sector, but also who stays, who progresses and who has the opportunity to shape its future.

title: DEWA study assesses PV cleaning robot performance and safety - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A research from Dubai Electricity and Water Authority have evaluated five autonomous PV cleaning robots under desert conditions. The researchers found cleaning efficiencies of 69% to 99%, while also identifying battery, corrosion, ingress-protection and mechanical reliability issues.
Lior Kahana
14 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Utility-scale
The different robots | Image: Dubai Electricity and Water Authority
A research team from the United Arab Emirates’
Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA)
has evaluated the cleaning performance of several PV cleaning robots in a desert environment. The team also outlined operation and maintenance recommendations for stakeholders based on the results.
Bhaduri added that the team evaluated the durability and operational reliability of the robots themselves under real desert conditions, identifying practical vulnerabilities associated with high temperatures, batteries, ingress protection, electronics, mechanical alignment and material degradation. “Based on these field observations and industry feedback, we further proposed a practical checklist for evaluating robotic PV cleaners before deployment,” she added.
Overall, the study evaluated five autonomous dry-cleaning robots. Robots A and B used bristle-based brushes and operated on fixed-tilt PV systems in a two-in-portrait configuration. Robot A weighed 48 kg, while Robot B weighed 45 kg. Robots C, D and E were deployed on single-axis trackers in a one-in-portrait configuration and weighed less than 40 kg. Robots C and E used microfiber cloth-based cleaning systems, while Robot D used bristles. Robots C and D were produced by the same manufacturer, allowing a direct comparison of the two cleaning materials. The systems were manufactured in China, India and Greece by undisclosed companies.
All robots were tested at the DEWA Cleaning Test Facility, located next to the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park in Dubai. The test field comprised 164 crystalline-silicon PV modules rated between 445 W and 505 W, including monofacial PERC glass-backsheet modules and bifacial PERC glass-glass modules. Outdoor performance monitoring was carried out from July 22, 2024, to August 26, 2025, with occasional laboratory I–V, reflectance, electroluminescence (EL), dark lock-in thermography (DLIT) and microscopy measurements.
“Daily robotic cleaning reduced soiling rates from approximately 0.14–0.33% per day to below 0.02% per day,” Bhaduri said. “The evaluated robots achieved cleaning efficiencies of 69–99%, while EL and DLIT testing found no robot-induced cell cracks or electrical defects over two years.”
Bhaduri added, however, that repeated cleaning caused minor wear to the anti-reflective coating, with greater abrasion observed for bristle-based cleaning than for cloth-based cleaning. “We have further identified important safety and reliability concerns, including battery overheating, inadequate ingress protection, corrosion, frame misalignment and UV degradation of polymer components,” she added.
In conclusion, the group proposed a 12-point checklist for evaluating PV cleaning robots before deployment. Key recommendations include using IEC 62133-certified batteries with thermal management, ensuring at least IP65/IP66 protection for electronic components, using UV- and corrosion-resistant materials, conducting PV-specific abrasion testing, integrating SCADA-based fault and cleaning verification, and monitoring module misalignment and frame deformation.
The study “
Performance and safety evaluation of PV cleaning robots in desert environment
” was published in
Solar Energy.
