title: PVFarm rolls out RE STACK software for utility-scale BESS planning - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The new tool works across geographies, manufacturer, and sites, and is design to make site planning both faster and comprehensive.
Tristan Rayner
14 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Image: PVFarm
US-based PVFarm, which traditionally has offered large-scale solar PV project design and planning tools, has moved into the energy storage market with a new tool called RE STACK.
The new platform by the software company, founded in 2001, has now launched for commercial use and offers detailed utility-scale battery energy storage (BESS) layout exploration across manufacturers, sites, and locations.
Among the promised planning solutions for BESS projects, RE STACK tackles manufacturer specifications to explore site layouts, road concepts, and medium-voltage collection topologies before detailed engineering begins, which the company claims saves time and effort.
Maksim Markevich, chief technology officer at PVFARM, answered a range of questions from ESS News after the launch of the BESS tool.
ESS News: What common pain points is RE STACK aiming to solve, and are there real-world examples that may be of interest to ESS News readers?
Maksim Markevich:
RE STACK addresses a simple problem: early-stage BESS design is still highly manual and fragmented.
Engineers often move between manufacturer specifications, spreadsheets, CAD, mapping tools and previous projects to answer interconnected questions:
How much equipment fits? Which block configuration works best? What clearances are required? How should roads be arranged? Where should auxiliary equipment go? How does MV collection change with the layout?
The challenge is not creating one layout; it is exploring enough credible alternatives, quickly enough, to make better early decisions.
One battery manufacturer recently tested RE STACK using customer-provided site boundaries to understand how much equipment it could fit and ultimately supply. Its existing workflow relied primarily on AutoCAD and considerable manual effort. With RE STACK, the team could configure its BESS blocks, test layouts quickly, and then export a layered DXF to continue working within its established engineering workflow.
In another test, a large irregular site showed how something as simple as road orientation could materially change the amount of equipment that fits. Instead of manually rebuilding alternatives, the software can explore road-grid angle and position together to find better-performing layouts.
That is the value we are trying to create: more credible options in less time, while keeping engineers in control of the assumptions.
Is this for a particular region or geography, or is it cross-region and therefore takes into account relevant standards and regulations?
RE STACK is designed to work across regions rather than being tied to one geography.
The software is configurable. Engineers can define equipment dimensions, clearances, setbacks, road dimensions, block arrangements and other project-specific requirements. This allows the same platform to represent different manufacturers, clients, jurisdictions, and project requirements.
We deliberately separate this from automated compliance. RE STACK does not claim to interpret every applicable fire, building, or permitting code and certify that a design is compliant. Engineers remain responsible for selecting and validating the requirements appropriate to their project.
Our job is to make those requirements easier to represent, change, and test—and to keep the assumptions behind the layout transparent.
How does someone learn the software, and is dedicated training required?
We designed RE STACK as a self-service product, so dedicated training should not be required for the core workflow.
An engineer familiar with BESS can import a site, configure equipment and blocks, define roads and layout parameters, generate a layout, and start adjusting it interactively without first becoming a software specialist.
More advanced workflows naturally require some guidance—for example, creating custom equipment configurations, defining individual clearances, importing geolocated KML, KMZ or DXF boundaries, or representing phased deployment.
Our principle is simple: learning the software should be the easy part.
Has RE STACK already adapted to changing requirements during the development process?
Constantly. The product has been developed alongside engineers, developers, EPCs, utilities and equipment manufacturers testing it on real projects. Many capabilities in RE STACK today came directly from cases where our original assumptions did not match how projects are actually designed.
Roads are a good example. Early versions were relatively simple. Real sites pushed us toward more flexible road-grid tuning, site zones, rotation controls and manual adjustments.
The same happened with BESS blocks. We initially thought a library of common configurations might be enough. Manufacturer examples quickly showed otherwise. Batteries, PCS units and transformers are packaged and connected in many different ways, and even a single project may require different arrangements across the site.
That led us toward a flexible block configurator where engineers can define and save their own equipment and configurations rather than being constrained by our assumptions.
This feedback loop is central to how we build RE STACK. BESS is evolving too quickly for engineering software to assume today’s requirements will remain fixed.
Does RE STACK work with any BESS manufacturer, a specific subset, or some other arrangement?
RE STACK is manufacturer-agnostic.
Instead of restricting engineers to a fixed equipment catalog, users can define equipment dimensions, capacities, clearances and block arrangements themselves, then save those configurations for reuse.
This matters because BESS products are changing quickly. Different suppliers package batteries, PCS units, transformers and auxiliary equipment differently, and new configurations continue to enter the market.
We want engineers to be able to model the equipment they are actually evaluating rather than wait for a software vendor to add it to a catalog.
What does RE STACK cost?
RE STACK has a free trial, so engineers can test it on a real project before deciding whether it is useful for their workflow.
The current subscription price is visible directly in the product. However, we are still early in the commercial rollout, and we expect pricing to evolve over the next six months as we learn more about how different customers use RE STACK and what pricing model best supports the market.
Our priority right now is: make it easy for developers and engineers to try the product, get value from it, and help us shape where it goes next.
Following the interview,
ESS News
signed up to use RE STACK. Current pricing after the free trial is billed at $2,880/year, broken down into $240 per seat/month.

title: Partial U.S. eclipse produced similar daily solar energy losses to higher-obscuration European locations - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
In a new weekly update for
pv magazine
, Solcast, a DNV company, reports that the Aug. 12 solar eclipse caused highly variable irradiance losses across Europe and North America, shaped by obscuration, cloud cover, and the timing of the eclipse.
However, eclipse-related power-market impacts varied much more, showing that irradiance loss or obscuration alone is not a reliable predictor of electricity-price effects.
14 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Americas
Utility-scale
Total eclipse at 18:29:32 UTC as seen from León, Spain | Image: ZarlokX, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
The Aug. 12 solar eclipse produced sharply different levels of obscuration across the North Atlantic. The path of totality crossed through Greenland, Iceland and Spain, while much of Western Europe observed over 80% obscuration and levels remained below 20% across the north-eastern United States. Despite the contrast daily irradiance losses were similar in some European and North American locations, according to analysis using the Solcast API. This similarly did not hold true for cloud and electricity market impacts which varied more greatly.
While Solcast’s pre-event analysis showed the irradiance losses under clear-sky conditions, we can now see how cloud conditions on the day reduced the impact in some regions and what the final result was.
As noted in clear sky irradiance losses, peak obscuration alone did not determine the daily eclipse-related loss. Some eastern North American locations experienced less than 20% peak obscuration but still recorded daily irradiance losses greater than European locations where obscuration exceeded 80%. Montreal followed this pattern, with cloud cover reducing its observed daily eclipse-related loss below the clear-sky estimate, while the remaining loss was still comparable with several much higher-obscuration European locations. The eclipse occurred near midday in North America, when irradiance levels were relatively high, but just before sunset in western Europe when irradiance was already declining.
This drop was mitigated in some locations by cloud, which reduced the absolute irradiance lost to the eclipse, although did also ruin the view. Most western European locations showed little difference between observed-cloud and clear-sky losses, due to limited cloud cover during the eclipse period. Iceland, Ireland and the north of the UK were some of the few exceptions. Reykjavik was particularly notable. Although Iceland lay within the path of totality and Reykjavik would have lost more than 5% of its daily solar resource under clear skies, cloud cover reduced the additional eclipse-related loss to below 1%. The impact on power market outcomes was less straightforward. While the eclipse reduced available irradiance across multiple regions, price impacts depended on prevailing market conditions, including demand, available generation and operating margins.
Spain experienced some of the highest obscuration among the markets examined. During the 19:30 to 21:15 CEST eclipse period, OMIE day-ahead prices were approximately €175 ($202.1)/MWh to €250/MWh. Prices were approximately 10% higher than the typical summer weekday range for that time of day, but remained below the highest prices recorded during summer 2026.
France showed a much larger departure from its summer weekday distribution during the period that coincided with the eclipse. Prices moved above the weekday median and interquartile range, although the comparison does not isolate the eclipse as the cause.
New York provides the eastern North American comparison, with NYISO’s Hudson Valley zone used as a representative example of market conditions during the eclipse period.
In contrast to the European examples, day-ahead pricing in NYISO’s Hudson Valley zone remained within the typical range of summer weekday values throughout the eclipse period. Prices during the eclipse were broadly aligned with the summer weekday distribution.
Taken together, the results show that eclipse obscuration or irradiance lost was not areliable indicator of market impacts.
produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary
AI/ML algorithms
. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

title: Vikram Solar inaugurates 6 GW solar PV module factory in India - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Vikram Solar has inaugurated a 6 GW solar PV module manufacturing plant at Gangaikondan in Tirunelveli district, Tamil Nadu. Following the commissioning of the new production line, the company’s total solar PV module manufacturing capacity has increased to 15.5 GW per year.
Uma Gupta
14 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Highlights
Vikram Solar
Vikram Solar has inaugurated a 6 GW solar PV module manufacturing plant at Gangaikondan in Tirunelveli district, Tamil Nadu. The facility was inaugurated by Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Thiru C. Joseph Vijay.
Following the commissioning of the new 6 GW module production line, Vikram Solar’s total solar PV module manufacturing capacity has increased to 15.5 GW per year.
Located on a nearly greenfield campus, the 6 GW manufacturing facility is expected to create employment opportunities for more than 800 skilled professionals in the region.
The Gangaikondan campus is planned to expand beyond module manufacturing in the coming years to include solar cell, wafer, and ingot manufacturing, bringing key stages of the solar PV value chain together at a single location.
As part of its broader manufacturing expansion, Vikram Solar plans to establish 9 GW of solar cell manufacturing capacity by fiscal year 2027, increasing this to 12 GW by fiscal year 2028. A 9 GW wafer and ingot facility is also planned at the site. The company said the expansion is aimed at deepening domestic value addition, strengthening supply-chain resilience and creating sustained industrial and employment opportunities in Tamil Nadu.
“Tamil Nadu offers a strong industrial foundation, skilled talent and a progressive environment for manufacturing-led growth. Our investment here reflects our long-term commitment to the State, to local employment and to building a more self-reliant clean energy value chain in India,” said Gyanesh Chaudhary, chairman & managing director, Vikram Solar. “The Gangaikondan facility is an important step in our journey towards building an integrated solar manufacturing ecosystem.”

title: Ireland records 1,258 MW grid-scale solar generation peak ahead of eclipse - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The solar coaster came to Ireland this week as EirGrid recorded an all-time high peak generation followed two days later by generation lows of 8 MW during the historic solar eclipse on August 12.
Blathnaid O’Dea
14 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
Image: Benlisquare, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
The sun doesn’t normally have a very busy week in Ireland but a record-breaking generation day for solar on the national grid followed two days later by a solar eclipse made this week different.
Data from Irish transmission systems operator (TSO) EirGrid showed grid-scale solar generation peaked at 1,258 MW just before 1 p.m. on Tuesday, 11 August – the highest level recorded so far. During that time, solar accounted for around a third of all electricity usage nationally.
“This new daily peak comes on the back of EirGrid’s most recent monthly report – showing that July was a record month for solar energy in Ireland,” said Irish Minister for Climate, Energy, and the Environment, Darragh O’Brien.
“We currently have over 8 GW of renewable electricity generation capacity connected to the network. To put that into perspective, we have added approximately 5 GW of new renewable electricity generation capacity in just ten years,” he said.
Most of this renewable electricity comes from wind, but solar deployment has experienced very positive momentum. Irish developers PCRE, Harmony Solar and Activ8 to name a few are growing their project portfolios fast across their respective sectors and foreign developers such as ILOS, Perigus Energy (formerly Orsted) and Statkraft are committed to investments there.
“Just over 10 years ago there were 2 MW of solar in Ireland. Now there are over 2.6 GW,” O’Brien pointed out, adding that it is fitting record solar generation occurred the same week Europe witnessed “a historic solar eclipse” on Wednesday.
Europe’s TSOs expected the solar eclipse to
temporarily reduce
solar generation on August 12 but were not concerned about overall electricity supply.
In Ireland, EirGrid recorded a grid-scale generation peak of 1,090 MW at 1.45 p.m., ahead of the forecast peak at 1,038 MW.
At 6.15 p.m., when the moon moved across the sun, grid-scale solar was generating 532 MW. This fell to 202 MW by 6.45 p.m. and plummeted to 8 MW at the height of the eclipse 30 minutes later.
After the moon began moving away from the sun, grid-scale solar generation statistics showed gradual improvement, reaching 51 MW by 7.30 p.m. and 83 MW at 7.45 p.m.
Ronan Power, CEO of Solar Ireland, said that while the eclipse only lasted a couple of hours it gave “a lovely snapshot of the much bigger solar community that has developed across Ireland” as people became citizen scientists for the day tracking solar generation on their phones and commenting on the eclipse, encouraged by Solar Ireland’s campaign, which Power described as “a bit of fun” and an opportunity for people to share what their rooftop systems were generating throughout the event.
“You could actually see the eclipse in Ireland’s solar generation curve, which is quite remarkable,” said Power.

title: Watch: Deep Robotics humanoid robot conquers real-world concrete stairs, rough terrain
content: Deep Robotics has released new footage showing its DR02 humanoid robot climbing outdoor concrete stairs, highlighting the machine’s ability to handle challenging terrain and maintain dynamic movement. The latest demonstration comes as the Hangzhou-based robotics company enters a key phase in its development and commercialization efforts. By tackling uneven, demanding outdoor surfaces, the DR02 is positioned as a platform capable of performing more complex tasks in real-world settings. Recently, DEEP Robotics’ robot dog tracked Tibetan antelopes at 4,700 meters, capturing migration and feeding behavior while demonstrating robotic operation in extreme high-altitude terrain. DR02 tackles terrain The latest demonstration comes at a significant moment for the Hangzhou-based company. Deep Robotics has applied to raise about $367.4 million through an initial public offering on Shanghai’s STAR Market, with the application recently accepted. The planned listing comes as the company seeks to build on a major financial milestone: Deep Robotics reported its first-ever net profit in 2025, earning about $4.2 million. The timing makes the DR02 ’s development particularly important. As Chinese robotics companies compete to commercialize humanoid machines, investors are increasingly looking for evidence that these systems can move reliably in real-world environments rather than perform scripted demonstrations. The new footage highlights several aspects of the DR02’s mobility. The humanoid is shown climbing concrete stairs outdoors, while earlier demonstrations have shown it running across uneven grass, jumping over obstacles and navigating challenging terrain. Recently, the robot has also been shown carrying a fire extinguisher mounted on its back and operating around high-voltage electrical infrastructure, pointing toward Deep Robotics’ ambitions for industrial and hazardous-environment applications. DR02 built tough Deep Robotics’ DR02 is a 175-centimeter (5-foot-9-inch) industrial humanoid designed for all-weather outdoor and factory operations. The standard DR02 weighs 143 pounds (65 kilograms) with its battery and has 68-centimeter (26.8-inch) arms. It has 31 degrees of freedom, including six per leg, seven per arm, and three at the waist. A dexterous hand is optional. For mobility, the robot has a normal walking speed of 1.5 meters per second (3.4 mph) and a laboratory-tested maximum speed of 4 m/s (8.9 mph). It can continuously climb stairs up to 25 centimeters (9.8 inches) high and handle slopes of up to 20 degrees. Its dual-arm payload is 22 pounds (10 kilograms). The DR02’s defining feature is its full-body IP66 dust- and water-resistance rating, allowing operation from -4°F (-20°C) to 131°F (55°C). Its perception system combines one LiDAR, three depth cameras, and one wide-angle camera, while computing is handled by an industrial 64-bit octa-core processor with 16GB memory and 128GB storage, plus an AI processor providing up to 275 TOPS. The robot uses a 20Ah, 1,440Wh swappable battery. Deep Robotics also provides modular quick-disassembly hardware, allowing components including the forearms, full arms, and legs to be replaced rapidly. According to Deep Robotics,  DR02 is designed for industrial, hazardous, and outdoor applications, including factory operations, equipment inspection, emergency response, infrastructure maintenance, and work around high-voltage electrical systems. Its rugged construction, all-weather protection, stair-climbing ability, and advanced perception make it suited to environments that are difficult or dangerous for human workers.

title: New X-ray tech snaps 1000 battery images per second to reveal failures
content: Battery engineers could soon be able to see exactly what happens inside a lithium-ion cell when it fails. On August 13, Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for High-Speed Dynamics, Ernst-Mach-Institut (Fraunhofer EMI), announced that its high-speed X-ray technology is being prepared for industrial use with Volkswagen’s battery company, PowerCo.The system captures what happens inside large prismatic battery cells as they operate under harsh conditions. Fraunhofer EMI describes it as a “globally unique high-speed X-ray system.”This technology could help European automakers better study battery safety and improve future cell designs.X-rays capture hidden battery changesBattery failures can happen quickly, which makes it hard for engineers to know exactly what goes on inside a cell. Usually, they rely on computer simulations, destructive tests, or measurements from outside the cell.Fraunhofer EMI’s system lets researchers see inside the cell as it is tested. It uses high-performance X-ray imaging along with a special battery test chamber and sensors that simultaneously monitor temperature, pressure, voltage, and gas flow.The system can record up to 1,000 images every second. This allows researchers to watch gas forming, materials moving, and cracks spreading in great detail.“Recording up to 1,000 images per second, it reveals processes such as gas formation, material displacement, and crack propagation inside the cell at extremely high resolution—events that until now have remained hidden from view.”The Fraunhofer EMI has developed a globally unique high-speed X-ray system that makes dynamic processes inside large-format prismatic cells visible in real time for the first time. (Image credit: Fraunhofer EMI)Built to withstand thermal runawayThe technology also needed to handle the harsh conditions that occur when lithium-ion batteries enter thermal runaway. Fraunhofer EMI created a protective chamber to shield sensitive X-ray equipment and keep it safe during these tests.Dr Sebastian Schopferer, Head of Battery Safety at Fraunhofer EMI, said: “Our in-situ method allows us to see what happens inside a cell in fractions of a second—in real time and at the highest resolution. This fundamentally changes how we understand battery design and safety.”Fraunhofer EMI has already used the system to study how materials are ejected during thermal runaway and how failures spread in multi-cell battery setups. The institute said that several German automakers, including Volkswagen and Audi, have used this data.“The resulting data enables engineers to assess cell designs based on directly observed processes and refine simulation models with greater precision—delivering direct added value for product development and certification processes.”Still image from an X-ray video recorded during a nail penetration test of a prismatic lithium-ion cell. (Image credit: Fraunhofer EMI)PowerCo prepares industrial deploymentThe next step is to adapt the technology for use in industrial battery development. Fraunhofer EMI will share its expertise in materials research, battery testing, and high-speed imaging. PowerCo will offer production requirements and access to its cell designs.PowerCo said that results from the partnership are already helping to develop better production cells.A dedicated X-ray system is planned for PowerCo’s site in Salzgitter, Germany, by 2028. The system will work with different cell formats and battery chemistries, so it can keep up as battery technology evolves.A closer look at future battery cellsSpeaking about the new technology, HW Vassen, CTO at PowerCo, highlighted, “With in-situ high-speed X-ray imaging, we are taking battery research to a new level.”“For the first time, we can make the dynamic processes inside cells visible in real time and in slow motion. This unprecedented depth of insight allows us to optimize battery cell safety and design in a highly targeted way and bring innovations into industrial use much faster. Together with Fraunhofer EMI, we are advancing high technology made in Europe and are strengthening Europe’s role in the battery industry.”

title: CosmoCube satellite to probe cosmic dark ages from behind the Moon
content: A new suitcase-sized satellite has been designed to investigate the cosmic dark ages, which is the 150-million-year period between the Big Bang and the birth of the first stars. Dubbed CosmoCube, it will also explore the role of dark matter in early universe formation.Led by researchers at the University of Cambridge, the mission aims to detect the faint 21-centimeter radio line emitted by early hydrogen atoms operating at low frequencies (10–50 MHz), a signal never before directly observed.Moon as a shieldEarth’s ionosphere and radio interference (FM radio, telecommunications) block these low-frequency signals. For astronomers trying to listen for the faint, 13.5-billion-year-old signals of the early universe, Earth’s radio noise is like a heavy metal concert playing right outside a recording studio door.As a result, the team designed CosmoCube to hide behind the Moon.The UK-backed satellite will embark on a two-year mission around the Moon.Every two hours, CosmoCube will loop around the lunar far side. For 40 brief minutes, the Moon will block every piece of human chatter from Earth.“There’s no other place where you can get the sort of shielding you need to detect such a faint signal, while at the same time looking at the whole of space,” said Professor Eloy de Lera Acedo from Cambridge’s Cavendish Laboratory. “The far side of the Moon is really the only option: it solves multiple problems at once, opening a clear window to the very early universe.”Over a two-year mission, CosmoCube will gather 1,000 hours of data to map the universe’s transition from an empty, dark void into the complex cosmos seen today. Supported by funding from the UK Space Agency, researchers aim to launch the satellite within the next five years.Calibrating for precisionCosmoCube will use a newly unfolded, lightweight antenna during its far-side orbits. To ensure accuracy, an internal “Dicke switched” calibrator will continually toggle between the sky and reference sources to filter out satellite electronic noise. Once transmitted back to Earth, scientists will use Bayesian statistical methods alongside sky-response computer simulations to remove Galactic foreground emissions and instrument distortions.The satellite will also use cutting-edge RF-System-on-Chip (RFSoC) technology to power its miniature radiometer. Apart from mapping the pre-star universe, CosmoCube will also investigate how mysterious dark matter functioned in the early cosmos. Scientists hope to reveal its role as the gravitational force that pulled hydrogen together to form the very first stars and galaxies.“This emission from hydrogen after the Big Bang, but before the first stars, will hopefully allow us to understand the role of dark matter in the early universe, how it worked to pull together hydrogen into the first stars and galaxies,” said de Lera Acedo.The pristine radio-quiet zone on the far side of the Moon may soon become a crowded place like Earth’s orbit. As nations like the US and India plan increasingly ambitious lunar orbital and surface missions, human presence and satellite communications risk introducing new radio interference. This impending surge in lunar traffic makes time-sensitive missions like CosmoCube crucial to capturing the universe’s earliest faint signals before the quietest sanctuary in the solar system becomes noisy.

title: US Army picks six UGV makers for high-risk frontline logistics missions
content: The U.S. Army is moving to put autonomous ground vehicles into one of the most dangerous parts of the battlefield, selecting six companies to develop production-ready prototypes for missions that currently require soldiers to drive into exposed areas.The Infantry Last Tactical Mile (ILTM) initiative focuses on the stretch between rear support areas and the forward line of own troops (FLOT), where getting ammunition, equipment and supplies forward, or bringing casualties back, can expose personnel to enemy fire.The six selected companies are Maren-Go, Overland AI, Forterra, Hendrick’s Motorsports, American Rheinmetall and HDT. Each is expected to provide four prototype vehicles for Army testing, according to Breaking Defense, citing an Army spokesperson. Rather than simply building another remotely controlled vehicle, the Army wants systems capable of beyond-line-of-sight autonomous operation. The vehicles are intended to conduct logistical resupply, casualty evacuation and network-extension missions, potentially allowing troops to perform critical battlefield tasks without putting additional drivers or medics directly in harm’s way.The “last tactical mile”The concept borrows from a familiar logistics problem. Moving supplies from a large rear-area distribution point to a forward unit can be relatively straightforward until the final few miles. Those roads and trails are often where vehicles become vulnerable to artillery, drones, mines, and small arms fire.That makes the ILTM concept less about replacing conventional trucks and more about removing humans from particularly hazardous portions of the supply chain.The Army says the selected systems will need to support manned close-combat formations while operating autonomously beyond the operator’s direct line of sight.The approach also reflects a quickly occurring shift in military robotics. Autonomy is increasingly being treated as a means of changing how existing vehicles are used rather than simply as a new type of weapon.Six companies, different approachesThe Army has not publicly disclosed the vehicles that all six companies will submit, but some candidates are already known. According to Breaking Defense, American Rheinmetall is expected to provide its Mission Master SP-H, an unmanned tracked vehicle designed for autonomous logistics and other missions. Overland AI will provide its ULTRA platform, an autonomous off-road vehicle derived from Polaris’ RZR platform and equipped with Overland’s autonomy technology.Forterra has previously unveiled MESA, a logistics and casualty-evacuation vehicle based on the Polaris Ranger XD 1500. It combines Forterra’s AutoDrive autonomous driving system with its Vektor communications technology, which is designed to operate in low-bandwidth environments.The other three participants, Maren-Go, Hendrick’s Motorsports and HDT, have not publicly disclosed their intended ILTM vehicles. The variety is significant. Instead of committing immediately to a single vehicle architecture, the Army is effectively subjecting multiple approaches to the same test regime and allowing battlefield performance to determine which ones deserve further investment.From prototypes to soldiersThe selections are not yet a production order for an autonomous Army fleet. The companies are expected to receive formal prototype agreements in the coming weeks, followed by technical demonstrations and evaluations.Each vendor is expected to deliver four vehicles, after which the Army will assess how the systems perform under operationally relevant conditions. The decisive stage is planned for early 2027, when an Army unit will conduct an Operational Assessment. Feedback from soldiers will then help determine which platforms should move toward production.That testing will be particularly important because autonomy in a controlled demonstration is very different from autonomy in a battlefield environment. A useful system must navigate difficult terrain, maintain communications, operate when satellite or other links are disrupted, and respond appropriately when its route or mission changes.The Army’s objective is therefore not simply to create a vehicle that can drive itself. It is looking for a system that can keep logistics moving and evacuate casualties when sending a human crew into the same area would be unnecessarily dangerous.If the ILTM program succeeds, autonomous ground vehicles could become another layer of the Army’s battlefield logistics network, taking on some of the most exposed jobs while allowing soldiers to concentrate on the missions that still require human judgment.

title: Simple salt fix brings perovskite tandem solar cells to 29% efficiency
content: Researchers in Lithuania have increased tandem perovskite solar cell efficiency to more than 29 percent after modifying an ultra-thin molecular layer that transfers positive charge carriers within the device.Kaunas University of Technology (KTU) scientists and their international partners created a more stable interface between different layers of the solar cells. This reduced the corrosion and made it possible for the cells to maintain higher efficiency and performance. Kasparas Rakštys, PhD, a researcher at KTU, pointed out that these layers must be perfectly interconnected for the device to operate efficiently. “Simply put, a solar cell can be imagined as a multi-layered sandwich in which each layer is made of a different material and performs a specific function,” he added. The solution involved altering the molecular group responsible for bonding with the metal oxide layer. Instead of its conventional acidic form, they turned it into an ionic salt. With this new method, perovskite tandem solar cells achieved a power conversion efficiency of more than 29 percent.Protecting the interfacePerovskite solar cells are thin-film photovoltaic (PV) devices that use a perovskite material as the active layer. They’re considered a promising energy technology as they’re lightweight, flexible, and relatively cheap to manufacture. However, their performance can deteriorate when exposed to moisture, oxygen, and heat. A solar cell consists of several layers that must work together to collect and transport electrical charges. Problems at the interfaces between these layers can significantly affect the performance of the cell.Until recently, scientists relied on charge-transporting self-assembled monolayers (SAMs). Initially introduced in 2018, these are thin layers of molecules that act like molecular glue. They transport positive charge carriers, known as holes, toward an electrode. Nonetheless, Rakštys noted that a particular problem emerged over time. “Due to their acidic nature, these molecules can gradually corrode adjacent layers, creating defects at the interface that hinder charge transport,” he stressed. “As a result, the solar cell becomes less efficient and its operational lifetime is reduced.”That’s why the researchers decided to modify the part of the SAM molecule that attaches to the metal oxide contact layer. As reported, they chemically converted the molecules into neutral ionic salts.A molecular quick fix“In this study, we simply neutralized the acidic molecules by converting them into chemically neutral salts, creating a non-aggressive interface that allows the solar cell to operate much more stably and efficiently,” Rakštys stated, adding that the approach offers several technological benefits. The resulting salt molecules bind just as strongly to metal oxide surfaces. They are additionally water-soluble, which means that the layer can be deposited without relying on toxic solvents. Despite being only a few nanometers thick, the modified layer can have a great effect on how efficiently charges travel through the device.To test whether the solution could be applied in practice, the researchers worked together with partners in China. They showed that it does work on large-area modules. It produced a uniform, high-quality coating that’s suitable for more practical testingThe method was also tested in perovskite tandem solar cells, which use different light-absorbing layers to capture a broader portion of the solar spectrum. “Using our new approach, we achieved a power conversion efficiency greater than 29 percent in perovskite tandem solar cells – one of the highest values reported to date,” Rakštys concluded. He and his team now believe that the technology could eventually lead to more versatile solar devices, like cells added to building facades, windows, and textiles. They have already applied for a patent and are moving toward commercial use.The study has been published in the journal Nature Communications.

title: Ultra Maritime pairs two sonars to hunt submarines, underwater drones
content: Ultra Maritime showed off a new underwater surveillance system at the U.S. Navy’s 2026 Lanternfish exercise. The demonstration highlighted how the company’s Sea Spear passive sonar and SSQ-125B active sonobuoy can work together to find unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs).The demonstration focused on the use of autonomous systems for counter-UUV and anti-submarine missions. Sea Spear continuously listened for underwater activity without sending out signals, while the SSQ-125B used active sonar to help locate targets.The company said this exercise was an important step in proving their acoustic system for ongoing monitoring in challenging maritime areas. This setup could help naval forces keep track of underwater activity over wide regions.Two sonar systems share the workloadSea Spear provides the passive sensing element of the architecture. It is designed to remain deployed and monitor underwater areas for acoustic signatures associated with potential targets.The SSQ-125B brings active sensing to the sys. Its sonar can help pinpoint where an underwater object is once the passive sensors detect activity.Ultra Maritime describes the SSQ-125B as its latest generation of active sonobuoy technology. The company said it is the only active sonobuoy of its kind and is designed and manufactured exclusively by Ultra Maritime.Pairing the two systems gives operators access to different forms of acoustic information. Passive sensing can support persistent monitoring, while active sonar can provide more information needed to localize a target.Built around a distributed underwater networkThis demonstration is part of Ultra Maritime’s “Ocean of Things” concept. The plan is to use a network of underwater sensors that can be launched from both manned and unmanned platforms.Rather than using just one sensor, this system spreads sensors across the area. Many underwater nodes can work together to give a full picture of what is happening below the surface.The company believes this method is helpful for missions where underwater threats are hard to spot and track for long times. Adding more sensors can also expand the area covered by the network.Designed for wider maritime missionsUltra Maritime is building this system for different maritime security uses. It could be used to monitor ports, guard important infrastructure, and watch over key waterways.The system could also help monitor busy sea routes and support special operations. It is also meant for long-term monitoring, especially where underwater activity needs to be tracked all the time.The autonomous nature of the concept could reduce the need for crewed platforms to remain directly over a surveillance area. Sensors deployed from different platforms could instead contribute information to a broader underwater monitoring network.Lanternfish puts the concept to the testAt the 2026 Lanternfish exercise, the firm tested Sea Spear and SSQ-125B as parts of a networked detection system. The test examined how passive and active methods could work together to detect UUV targets.The exercise gave a real-world setting to test this combined approach. It also showed how each sonar system could be part of a bigger, self-running surveillance network.Ultra Maritime sees this combined system as the base for future undersea missions. By using both ongoing passive monitoring and active tracking, the company aims to improve its ability to detect and track underwater threats in challenging maritime environments.

title: New marine battery offers double energy density for electric vessels
content: Direct liquid cooling is moving into ship engine rooms with the introduction of the IMMERSIO Matrix. This energy storage system is designed to solve the primary technical challenges of maritime electrification. In this setup, developed by Taiwan-based XING Mobility, every lithium cell is fully submerged in an electrically non-conductive dielectric liquid. The fluid absorbs heat directly from the surface of each cell as soon as it is generated. “The coolant inherently suppresses thermal runaway, eliminates cell-to-cell propagation, and removes the ignition pathways that exist in air-cooled and cold-plate-cooled designs,” explained the company in a press release.Because the liquid controls temperatures effectively, the battery can sustain a continuous 3C discharge rate. “For fast ferries, port service vessels and any duty cycle built around hard acceleration and rapid charging between trips, this is the performance level that finally makes battery-electric propulsion a true replacement for diesel,” added the press release.The immersion-cooled system supports these heavy-duty cycles without overheating, providing a viable electric alternative to conventional marine diesel engines.Energy density optimization for scalabilityThe architecture also removes the need for bulky cooling plates, air ducts, and wide safety gaps between individual modules. As a result, the cell-to-pack configuration doubles both the gravimetric and volumetric energy density compared to standard marine batteries. “XING delivers twice the energy density of conventional marine batteries, offering more usable energy per kilogram and significantly more per cubic meter,” highlighted the company.This compact design is especially useful for vessel retrofits, where engineers must install electric systems inside existing engine rooms without reducing space for cargo or passengers.The hardware platform comes in scalable capacities between 60 kWh and 400 kWh and is currently undergoing the formal classification process for DNV marine certification.Step toward real-world deploymentsThe system will make its official European debut at the Electric & Hybrid Marine Expo in Amsterdam this June. The rollout targets European fleet operators working to meet strict regional environmental rules, including the FuelEU Maritime framework and the EU Emissions Trading System.To handle regional engineering, installation, and field service across Europe, XING Mobility is partnering with Nordic Booster AS. “We chose XING because their immersion-cooled architecture is, simply put, the safest and most power-dense battery system available for marine use today,” noted Trond Skaufel, CEO of Nordic Booster.The underlying battery platform is already operating on the water. In Taiwan, the zero-emission vessel Porrima P111 uses the immersion-cooled pack in open-ocean conditions. In Europe, Austrian electric-boat maker Smart IQ completed integration and functional system tests on its newest vessel in late April 2026.XING Mobility set up a dedicated mass-production facility for immersion battery hardware in 2024. The company builds its systems around a unified architecture that combines fluid cooling, physical protection, electrical controls, and safety mechanisms into one package. “The platform has since been extended across commercial vehicles, agricultural machinery, marine applications, energy storage, and AI data center infrastructure,” concluded the press release.

title: Damaged EV battery repair could be made safer with modular covers
content: The global solar boom could leave behind as much as 402 million tonnes (443 million tons) of discarded photovoltaic panels by 2060, creating a waste crisis that threatens to undermine the clean-energy transition.The warning comes from researchers in China, Australia, and Sweden, who examined how different regions could manage the rapidly growing stream of retired panels.The study found that recycling this waste could produce up to $935.5 billion in cumulative net economic benefits while preventing billions of tonnes of emissions. However, researchers warned that poorer countries could carry a disproportionate environmental burden without access to recycling technology, infrastructure, and investment.A 402-million-tonne waste problemSolar panels typically remain operational for decades, but the rapid expansion of photovoltaic capacity means increasingly large numbers will soon reach the end of their useful lives. The researchers estimate that cumulative global PV waste could reach between 297 million and 402 million tonnes by 2060.High-income regions are expected to dominate solar waste generation until around 2040. After that, upper-middle-income countries are likely to take the lead, with China emerging as the largest individual contributor.China alone could produce between 112.8 million and 160.5 million tonnes of discarded panels by 2060, accounting for as much as 39.9 percent of the global total. India could generate another 26.8 million to 35.2 million tonnes.“Solar power is essential to the transition to a low-carbon energy system, but we cannot ignore what happens to solar panels at the end of life,” said study co-author Jian Zuo from Adelaide University.“If we plan for recycling now, this growing waste stream can become a valuable source of materials rather than an environmental burden,” he added. Waste could become a valuable resourceThe team evaluated 1,708 recycling scenarios covering 32 regions. Its model incorporated recycling methods, changing material prices, international trade, technological development, and government subsidies.Solar panels contain recoverable materials such as silicon, silver, copper, aluminum, and tellurium. They can also contain hazardous metals, including lead and cadmium, which may pose environmental risks when panels are improperly dumped or processed.The analysis found that combining recycling technologies suited to individual regions with outsourced processing could generate between $529.1 billion and $935.5 billion in cumulative net benefits by 2060. This approach could also avoid up to 3.32 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions.Poorer regions risk being left behindOutsourcing waste to countries with advanced recycling facilities may lower costs and emissions, but it could also concentrate profits in wealthier and more technologically developed markets. Low-income regions may consequently receive only a marginal share of the economic gains.“The cheapest or most efficient recycling pathway globally is not necessarily the fairest,” Zuo said.“If developing regions are left without the technology, infrastructure or investment needed to recycle solar panels, they risk missing out on the economic benefits while potentially carrying more of the environmental burden.”The researchers proposed gradually declining subsidies as one possible solution. Financial support would initially help recycling industries develop before being reduced as recovered materials and improving technologies make operations commercially viable.The study was published in the journal Nature.

title: Damaged EV battery repair could be made safer with modular covers
content: A research initiative called the E-Track project has published new design guidelines to standardize electric vehicle batteries. When an electric vehicle crashes, firefighters face a dangerous guessing game. The lack of standardized battery design across automakers leaves emergency crews guessing when faced with a smoking vehicle. Even when an EV appears to be turned off or inactive after a crash, damaged packs can still hold high levels of dangerous electrical energy. To make matters worse, most manufacturers glue their battery housings together with heavy thermal pastes. The design makes production cheap. It makes repairs nearly impossible. A single dent often forces mechanics to throw away the entire unit. This practice of replacing entire units may soon come to an end.Led by the Graz University of Technology (TU Graz) alongside the University of Graz and industry leaders, the project delivers an interesting finding: saving just 8 percent of a damaged battery’s cells makes a repair-friendly design economically and environmentally worthwhile. “Our work shows that safety, efficiency and recyclability can be improved together through well-thought-out design,” said Markus Fasching, project manager from the Vehicle Safety Institute at TU Graz.Alternative architecturesThe increasingly complex interactions among electrical performance, thermal behavior, and mechanical safety in EV traction batteries have long suffered from a lack of uniform design standards. It complicates recycling efforts.Battery cells make up roughly 75 percent of a pack’s total weight. These cells account for most of the battery‘s financial and environmental value. However, current manufacturing methods treat these massive, resource-heavy components as single-use items. To fix this, the E-Track team analyzed two alternative architectures: modular covers with heat pads and liquid-cooled sealed enclosures. In the first case, replacing permanent adhesive with detachable covers and dry thermal pads allows technicians to open the unit without destroying it. Then, using an electrically insulating oil for heat dissipation inside a screwed housing. Technicians can easily unbolt the casing, isolate damaged cells, and swap them out safely.Advanced safety diagnosticsDismantling a damaged battery is only half the battle; knowing which cells are safe to keep is the real challenge. A minor crash can cause internal micro-shorts. These tiny flaws show no immediate outer damage, yet they can trigger delayed fires days after an accident.To catch these hidden threats, the researchers developed diagnostic tools using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy paired with virtual multiphysical models.The technology acts like an X-ray, letting technicians spot internal defects early and safely salvage healthy cells.Several automotive manufacturers are already exploring follow-up projects. As regulatory bodies push for stricter circular-economy laws, these guidelines could soon serve as the foundation for global battery standards, transforming a major fire hazard into a repairable asset.The need for recovering cells Funded by the Austrian Research Promotion Agency (FFG), the E-Track guidelines were initially tested on electric two-wheelers. However, the core physics and diagnostic models apply directly to passenger cars and commercial trucks.In today’s time of massive material demand, cell reuse is key because discarding an entire battery pack wastes massive amounts of essential raw materials like lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, copper, and aluminum. These are both ecologically damaging to extract and economically costly to refine. In some cases, non-damaged cells salvaged from crashes could be used in second-life applications. For instance, it can be repurposed for stationary grid energy storage, renewable energy backup, or industrial equipment, extending their useful lifespan and reducing overall environmental impact.

title: Chinese doctor solves decades-old math problem with help from ChatGPT
content: Jin Shanmu is a postdoctoral researcher at the Peking Union Medical College in Beijing, China, and also the cynosure of mathematicians from around the globe after he proved the famous Crouzeix’s conjecture with a little bit of help from ChatGPT. The math problem had troubled mathematicians for over two decades but was solved by Jin after the release of OpenAI’s latest reasoning model. While most people have looked at the availability of tools like ChatGPT and Claude to get away from their dreary work, for some like Jin Shanmu, it has opened up new opportunities for learning and discovery. The lazy ones among us ask AI tools to make presentation slides or give us a summary of a long memo the HR sent last week. Still, Jin, who has limited math education, was using the tool to research transcranial ultrasounds. If the sound of the technical term is making you look for something more palatable to read, know this first: Jin is a doctor, but he graduated with geology as his undergraduate major. So before stumbling across a famous math problem, Jin put himself through medical school and then began research using ultrasound scans of the brain, where he eventually did something incredible. What is Crouzeix’s Conjecture? Crouzeix’s Conjecture is a problem about matrices, which are typically used to solve linear equations or handle large amounts of data in computer science or physics. Matrices store values in a rectangular grid of numbers or symbols. These matrices can use mathematical operations like addition, subtraction, and multiplication among themselves and lead to the formation of new matrices that store the result of the operation in them. About two decades ago, French mathematician Michel Crouzeix posited that any function applied to a matrix is no larger than twice the function’s maximum value. While abstract, it has been a hurdle for mathematicians ever since. With the advent of large language models (LLMs) and tools like ChatGPT, mathematicians too began using them to solve such problems that have remained unsolved for years. Alex Townsend, a mathematician at Cornell University, and Anne Greenbaum, a professor at the University of Washington, too were using GPT models to solve Crouzeix’s Conjecture for the past year but late last month, came across a surprise. When AI solves your problemsTownsend had been prompting AI to solve the Crouzeix’s Conjecture, but for this attempt on July 30, ChatGPT informed him that the problem had been solved three days ago. When Townsend dug deeper, he found a paper submitted by Jin in which he given a definitive answer for the math problem. Although the paper is not peer-reviewed, Townsend reviewed the manuscript and even shared it with Greenbaum and Crouzeix, who confirmed that Jin’s proof was correct. While this manuscript shows the thirst for knowledge that Jin has, it also showcases the capability of models like ChatGPT, which have helped him crack the math, even without highly specialized training in the subject. One can credit this to AI because earlier in May OpenAI confirmed that a general-purpose reasoning model it had tested internally was able to solve the planar unit distance problem, posed by Paul Erdos, a Hungarian mathematician, way back in 1945. Earlier this month, the company also listed 10 other mathematical problems that its upcoming model, Astra, has nearly solved or made major progress on. Competing AI company Anthropic, whose Claude model is widely used by businesses, also said the latest version of its model is attempting to solve the famous Riemann hypothesis, showing once again that AI could answer major math puzzles that have been pending for decades, the South China Morning Post reported.

title: LG and NVIDIA to build 80-MW computing facility and humanoid robot
content: South Korea’s LG is deepening its collaboration with U.S. chipmaker NVIDIA to develop humanoid robots, establish AI factory infrastructure, and build next-generation autonomous vehicle systems.The companies signed a memorandum of understanding at NVIDIA’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California, on August 13. Their plans include unveiling a bipedal humanoid in the first quarter of 2027 and completing an 80-MW AI factory in Cheonan, South Korea, by the first half of 2028.“As our discussions have moved fast, our tasks and goals in AI Factory and Physical AI have become clear. We will accelerate the spread of AI by building industry-leading references,” said Kwang Mo Koo, Chairman and CEO of LG Corp.80-MW facility to advance physical AILG plans to establish an initial AI factory reference site powered by NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin computing platform in the first half of 2027. The project will combine NVIDIA’s DSX AI factory architecture with LG’s expertise in power systems, thermal management, data center design, and operations.Experience gained from the reference site will inform the construction of the larger 80-MW facility in Cheonan. Scheduled for completion during the first half of 2028, the AI factory will support the development of physical AI systems and robot foundation models.LG intends to validate an end-to-end AI factory package covering design, construction, and operations. The company could then offer these turnkey infrastructure packages to global technology customers looking to build large-scale AI computing facilities.Humanoid robot targets 2027 unveilingAlongside the computing infrastructure, LG is developing a next-generation bipedal humanoid powered by NVIDIA Jetson Thor for onboard processing, reasoning, and motion control. It is being built using the Isaac GR00T humanoid foundation model and NVIDIA’s Halos robotics safety system.LG Electronics, LG Innotek, and LG Energy Solution will contribute technologies including actuators, sensors, and batteries. The robot is expected to make its first public appearance in the first quarter of 2027.“The defining opportunity of physical AI is to give every machine the ability to understand the real world, reason and act safely alongside people — reshaping everyday life from the home and factory floor to the road,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA.LG will also deploy its wheel-based CLOiD robots at a washing machine factory in Tennessee before the end of 2026. Data from the production-line trials will be used to improve robot performance before deployments expand to other factories, commercial facilities, and homes.Partnership reaches future vehiclesThe companies will also develop an on-site robot data factory using LG CNS’s PhysicalWorks platform. It will continuously collect operational data, generate synthetic datasets, and support robot training, testing, and verification.In the mobility sector, LG plans to build a high-performance computing platform for AI-defined vehicles, powered by NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion. The platform will combine autonomous driving functions with LG’s infotainment and automotive software.A joint task force of technical and business specialists will oversee research, factory validation, and commercialization across the three areas.

title: 2,056 droids set to compete at World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing
content: Humanoid robots are set to take on a wider range of challenges in Beijing this month, as the second World Humanoid Robot Games is set to begin next week. The event brings together a record 2,056 machines from 666 teams representing 16 countries across six continents. The Aug. 22-26 event will feature newly introduced competitions in long jump, weightlifting, tug-of-war and table tennis, alongside other events. Organizers said the number of teams has increased 138 percent from last year, while robot participation has doubled.Robot games expandThe second World Humanoid Robot Games will see 666 teams and 2,056 robots from 16 countries across six continents competing in 51 events and 1,301 matches over five days.Co-hosted by the Beijing Municipal Government and China Media Group, the event has expanded from three days to five, with competition sessions scheduled in the afternoon and evening. This year’s games include 30 competitive events and 21 scenario-based events, compared with 26 events and 487 matches at the inaugural edition. The number of teams has increased 138 percent, while robot participation has quadrupled, reports China Daily.The United States, Germany, Japan and other countries with established robotics industries are sending teams. Brazil is participating with a five-member squad of Robot World Cup champions. China has 157 enterprises, 641 teams and 1,975 robots taking part. Teams from 27 Chinese universities are competing, with participants representing 30 provinces, autonomous regions, municipalities and special administrative regions.The scenario-based events have expanded from six last year and now cover nine settings: households, hotels, industrial facilities, emergency rescue, logistics, libraries, retail, office services and vehicle charging.Two new challenges focus on practical robotic capabilities. The Dexterous Hand Challenge includes tool assembly, powder weighing, block stacking, nail driving, bottle opening, unboxing, tweezer pick-up and cable connection. It evaluates areas including micro-distance vision, motion planning, force control and operational accuracy. The Integrated Five Challenge requires robots to perform dexterous operations, transfer objects stably and lift heavy loads while completing a 100-meter run.Stricter rules debutCompetition rules have also been tightened. Time limits for the 100-meter, 400-meter and 1,500-meter races have been reduced from three minutes to one minute, 15 minutes to five minutes, and 40 minutes to 15 minutes, respectively.Track and competitive events must be completed autonomously without remote control, except for the 100-meter and 400-meter obstacle races. In scenario events, fully autonomous completion receives a weight coefficient of 1.0, while remotely controlled completion is capped at 0.5, reports CGTN.In robot soccer, a goal counts only if at least two teammates have touched the ball during the build-up, encouraging coordinated play. Gold medals will be awarded across nine sessions. Twelve medal events are scheduled for Aug. 23. The opening evening will include a 7v7 soccer exhibition and preliminaries in the 100-meter and 400-meter races. Freestyle combat finals and the 5v5 soccer final are scheduled before the closing ceremony.Freestyle combat will feature eight sessions across 40-kilogram, 58-kilogram and 80-kilogram weight classes. Weightlifting, introduced this year, will award lightweight and heavyweight titles on Aug. 24. Dance participation has increased from 29 teams to 108, with street dance, ballroom and cheerleading competitions.The games will have 223 referees, including 28 international-level, 75 national-level and 120 first-tier officials. An expanded arbitration committee will handle disputes.

title: 19,000 feet beneath ocean surface: Deepest undersea mine planned
content: A report has revealed that the United States and Japan are exploring a major deep-sea mining project near Japan’s remote Minamitorishima Island, where rare-earth-rich deposits lie roughly 19,000 feet (6,000 metres) beneath the ocean surface. The project could become one of the deepest mining operations ever attempted and could mark a significant step in efforts by the U.S. and Japan to reduce their dependence on China for strategically important minerals. The project is about far more than mining. At its core is a struggle over who controls the supply chains that underpin electric vehicles, electronics, renewable-energy technologies, advanced manufacturing and defense systems.Rare-earth elements are a group of minerals with unusual magnetic, electrical and chemical properties. They are essential to the manufacture of high-performance magnets, motors, electronics and several advanced defence technologies.Rare-earth supply chainChina has built a commanding position across the rare-earth supply chain, particularly in processing and refining. That dominance has made diversification a strategic priority for the United States, Japan and other industrial economies.For Japan, the issue is especially sensitive. Tokyo has already experienced the risks associated with dependence on Chinese rare-earth supplies. The country has consequently spent years looking for alternative sources and technologies. Minamitorishima, a deposit thousands of metres below the Pacific, offers a potentially significant opportunity.Minamitorishima is a small, remote Japanese island located far out in the Pacific. Surveys have identified mineral-rich mud in the surrounding seabed, containing elements including yttrium, gadolinium and dysprosium. The mineral-bearing material is located at depths of approximately 6 kilometres. Recovering material from such depths presents enormous engineering challenges involving extreme pressure, long-distance pumping, specialized vessels and subsea equipment.Japan has already been working on the technology needed to overcome those obstacles. A Japanese government-backed programme has been developing a system designed to continuously lift rare-earth-rich mud from the seabed. Earlier plans envisaged testing the system at depths of around 6,000 metres and assessing whether it could eventually recover hundreds of tonnes of mud per day. Refining trial has been plannedThe immediate objective is not to suddenly create a giant commercial mine. Instead, Japan is attempting to prove that the technology works. A month-long extraction and refining trial has been planned as part of the country’s broader programme. The proposed system would lift seabed mud to the surface and then move the material for processing and separation in Japan. Japan has reportedly invested tens of billions of yen in the programme since 2018, illustrating how seriously Tokyo views the project. The next major question is whether the technology can move from an experimental demonstration to an economically viable mining operation.For the United States, the attraction is obvious: another potential source of critical minerals outside China’s dominant supply chain.The project is therefore emerging at the intersection of mining, technology and geopolitics. The U.S. wants to strengthen access to critical minerals, while Tokyo wants to build greater resilience into its own industrial supply chains.A successful US-Japan partnership could potentially go beyond simply extracting material from the seabed. It could contribute to the development of a broader mine-to-magnet supply chain, covering extraction, processing, refining and eventually the manufacture of high-value components. Analysts cited in reports on the project have described such integration as a potential way of reducing China’s influence over the sector.

title: New geometric design rule could build ultralow-energy computing systems
content: Researchers in the United States have identified a simple geometric design rule that could help engineers build reliable, ultralow-energy computing systems. The team also highlighted that the modern electronics rely on billions of tiny switches that consume electricity every time they turn on or off. So, researchers have been searching for alternatives that can perform the same tasks while using far less energy.Ultralow-energy computingNow, an Argonne-led study has uncovered a geometric rule that determines whether clusters of nanomagnets behave predictably or probabilistically as they relax toward a stable state. The finding challenges standard modeling assumptions and opens new possibilities for ultralow-energy computing.“What we have identified is a relationship between structure and function,” said Argonne Materials Scientist Hanu Arava, lead author of the study. ​“In our case, the structure is the geometric arrangement of the magnets with respect to each other, and the function is how energy moves through the system. We’ve shown that geometry alone can determine how energy moves through these magnetic systems and that insight gives us a new way to design computing devices.”To help explain the process, Arava compares it to dropping a ball from the top of a mountain. The ball naturally rolls downhill along the easiest route until it reaches the lowest point. Scientists call that route an energy-relaxation pathway — the path a system follows as it moves toward its most stable state. In the nanomagnet system, the magnets interact through their magnetic fields in a more complex way, but they follow the same basic principle: moving step by step toward the lowest-energy configuration, according to a press release.To uncover this relationship, the researchers studied a simple geometric progression at Argonne’s Center for Nanoscale Materials, a DOE Office of Science user facility. They began with four nanomagnets arranged in a Greek cross or plus sign, then rotated all four simultaneously until they formed a square. At intervals along the way, the team measured how the system relaxed toward its most stable state, as per the release.Intuitive framework for understanding energy relaxationPublished in Communications Materials, the study investigates the nature of intermediate states in a simple nanomagnet model consisting of four nanomagnets arranged onto a square plaquette. Through systematic exploration, researchers demonstrate how geometry influences energy relaxation pathways via multipolar analysis. “We elaborate on the nature of energy relaxation pathways, with direct consequences for understanding magnetic frustration and metastability in artificial spin ice structures. Our theoretical models are supported by experimental results from field-induced relaxation using Magnetic Force Microscopy measurements. This work provides an intuitive framework for understanding energy relaxation in artificial spin ice structures,” said researchers in the study.The team revealed that although the experiment involved just four nanomagnets, the result has broader implications. In larger magnetic devices, thousands of similar clusters would need to work together. The new findings give engineers a simple design principle: adjust the rotation angle of the magnets to tune how reliably they reach a predictable final state, according to researchers.

title: 10 bridges that transformed transportation and engineering
content: Bridges do much more than carry people from one side of an obstacle to another. The best ones have opened trade routes, connected cities, accelerated the construction of railways and roads, and introduced engineering techniques that changed what could be built afterward.From a cast-iron arch in the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution to suspension bridges spanning nearly 2 kilometers, these 10 structures stand out for their impact on transportation, society and engineering.1. Iron Bridge – EnglandCompleted in 1779, the Iron Bridge over England’s River Severn is widely recognized as the world’s first iron bridge. Its significance went far beyond a single crossing. It demonstrated that cast iron could be used for a major load-bearing structure at a time when the Industrial Revolution was transforming metal production. The bridge helped establish iron as a serious construction material and became an enduring symbol of industrial-era engineering. Its construction also helped stimulate development around Ironbridge, one of Britain’s most important industrial regions.2. Rialto Bridge – Venice, ItalyCompleted in 1591, Venice’s Rialto Bridge replaced a succession of wooden crossings and became the only pedestrian link between the two sides of the Grand Canal until the 19th century. Its single stone arch spans more than 28 meters, allowing boats to pass beneath, and thousands of timber piles support its foundations. More than a crossing, Rialto connected Venice’s political center with its commercial heart, helping people and commerce move through one of Europe’s great trading cities.3. Menai Suspension Bridge – WalesThomas Telford’s Menai Suspension Bridge, opened in 1826, was a landmark in both transportation and suspension-bridge engineering. Its 579-foot main span was the world’s longest when completed, allowing the strategically important road between London and Holyhead to cross the dangerous Menai Strait. More importantly, it demonstrated that suspension bridges could provide economical long spans for road traffic. The design influenced suspension-bridge development for decades and helped establish the form as a practical solution for major crossings.4. Brooklyn Bridge – New York, USWhen it opened in 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge was among the most ambitious infrastructure projects of the 19th century. John Roebling’s design combined a suspension system with stiffening elements and used steel cables, while enormous masonry towers supported the crossing. Its construction also advanced techniques for working underwater in pressurized caissons. The bridge physically connected Manhattan and Brooklyn, helping knit together what would become New York City. Its engineering influence was just as significant: the project demonstrated that enormous urban suspension bridges could be built and operated successfully.5. Forth Bridge – ScotlandOpened in 1890, Scotland’s Forth Bridge was the world’s earliest great multispan cantilever bridge. Its three enormous towers and cantilever arms produced spans of 521 meters, while about 54,000 tons of mild steel formed the structure. It was a landmark in the transition from iron to steel and demonstrated how cantilever construction could handle the heavy loads and long distances demanded by railways. It remains an active passenger and freight railway, more than 135 years after opening.6. George Washington Bridge – New York, USThe George Washington Bridge fundamentally changed expectations for suspension bridges when it opened in 1931. Its 3,500-foot main span was nearly twice that of its largest predecessor. Chief engineer Othmar Ammann developed a lighter stiffening-truss approach that offered greater flexibility and saved nearly $10 million. Perhaps more importantly, Ammann designed the structure with a future lower deck in mind. That foresight allowed the bridge to expand from six upper-level lanes to a massive 14-lane crossing, making it an influential example of designing infrastructure for future demand.7. Golden Gate Bridge – San Francisco, USThe Golden Gate Bridge opened in 1937 after engineers tackled strong winds, deep water, powerful tides, and a 1.7-mile-wide strait. Its 4,200-foot main suspension span was the world’s longest at the time. More than an engineering record, the bridge transformed transportation around San Francisco Bay. Marin County had previously depended heavily on ferries to connect with San Francisco. The project demonstrated that suspension bridges could span enormous waterways while remaining economically and structurally viable.8. Sydney Harbor Bridge – AustraliaCompleted in 1932, Sydney Harbor Bridge became the centerpiece of an integrated road and rail transportation system connecting the city’s northern and southern shores. Its massive steel arch was assembled from both sides of the harbor before being joined above the water. More than 53,000 tonnes of steel and six million rivets went into the structure. The bridge wasn’t simply an engineering landmark. It helped reshape modern Sydney by creating a permanent high-capacity crossing where ferries had previously dominated movement across the harbor.9. Akashi Kaikyo Bridge – JapanJapan’s Akashi Kaikyo Bridge pushed suspension engineering into a new era when it opened in 1998. Its 1,991-meter central span remains the longest of any suspension bridge. Engineers had to account for severe winds, earthquakes, powerful tidal currents and deep-water foundations. The bridge also became an important example of incorporating monitoring technology into long-span structures: sensors, GPS equipment and anemometers continuously track its behavior. Its engineering demonstrated how computer analysis, advanced materials and structural monitoring could work together on infrastructure at unprecedented scale.10. Millau Viaduct – FranceThe Millau Viaduct, opened in 2004, showed how modern bridge engineering could make a highway crossing appear almost impossibly light. The cable-stayed structure stretches across France’s Tarn Valley, with its tallest mast reaching about 343 meters. Its slender deck and multiple towers allow the highway to cross the deep valley without following the terrain below. The project demonstrated how modern materials, aerodynamic design, precision construction, and computer-assisted engineering could combine to create long, high crossings while minimizing the visual and physical footprint on the landscape.(Rather than ranking them purely by size or age, this list looks at bridges that had an outsized influence on transportation, construction technology, or the way engineers approached large infrastructure projects.)
